title: DASWeave: Weaving Evidence across Speaking Conditions for Multimodal Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Screening
summary: Multimodal screening for depression, anxiety, and stress in children and adolescents uses verbal and nonverbal behaviour. Most existing multimodal methods learn from a single recording or interview. Yet a participant's behaviour changes with the speaking condition, and these changes hold evidence that is invisible in a single recording. We propose DASWeave to bring this evidence into a neural network that encodes each response and then combines all responses of a participant. We train supervised trees to find which behavioural statistics matter for screening, both within each response and in how they change across conditions. We feed the tree outputs into the network both before and after this combination. We fine-tune a large language model to relate what a participant says to how they say it across conditions, and feed its representation into the network after the combination. The language model reads behaviour as text descriptions. We therefore derive additional training targets for the network from a multimodal large language model that takes in the audio-visual features directly. On the official hidden test set of the ACM Multimedia 2026 AdoDAS Grand Challenge (Track 1), DASWeave ranks second among 95 eligible teams. Its mean F1 is 27.1% higher than that of the official audio-visual baseline. It also has the highest mean AUROC among the top five teams. Ablation studies on the validation set show that the supervised trees and the fine-tuned language model contribute most to mean F1.

title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
summary: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.

title: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly evaluated by variance explained and ablation damage. We show how massive activations undermine both evaluations, and propose a correction. Massive activations cause up to 99.9% of activation variance to lie along the first principal component (PC1). Because the PC1 component has no unique sparse decomposition, each SAE run rebuilds it from a different set of features. These features dominate importance rankings: an average of 47 of the 50 most important features are unmatched in a separate run, compared with about 27 of a random 50. A dictionary can also report 99.96% of variance explained while leaving 33% of the variance outside PC1 unexplained. We bypass PC1 by training the SAE on activations with PC1 removed, then adding PC1 to the reconstruction. In affected models, the top-50 feature sharing rate rises from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%. At the same TopK sparsity, the resulting SAE degrades the model up to 44% less and reduces content reconstruction error by up to 33.9%.

title: Perspicacious: An Educational Intelligence Platform for Instructional Designers
summary: Designing effective instruction requires instructional designers to create assessment questions aligned with clearly defined knowledge components (KCs). These KCs represent specific knowledge or skills that students must acquire. This process is often time-consuming and relies heavily on expert labor. Although AI for education research has produced a growing body of automated question-generation and KC-discovery methods, few have moved beyond research prototypes into user-friendly tools that instructional designers can readily use. To bridge the research-to-practice gap, we developed and evaluated an educational intelligence platform that unifies question generation and KC discovery behind a single interface to support instructional content development. Named "Perspicacious," our platform aims to help instructional designers "see through" complex data and algorithms to derive instructional insights. A cost model calibrated on 17 production runs revealed a cost-time trade-off: extracting KCs from a 576-question bank cost US $1.98-4.11 and took 36-158 minutes to complete, depending on the budget. A formative, partially Wizard-of-Oz study with eight instructional designers found strong perceived usability (mean SUS 78.8) and surfaced concrete requirements that we treat as prerequisites for deployment.

title: Tabular Foundation Models in Financial Predictions
summary: This technical note introduces tabular foundation models (TFMs) to accounting research and evaluates their performance in one common benchmark task: predicting firms' next-year earnings changes. TFMs produce numeric predictions and learn in context, without post-release training or tuning, making them natural and easy to use for forecasting. The TFMs we study are pretrained on synthetic tabular data, so they avoid look-ahead bias from memorizing firms' outcomes. We compare Google Research's TabFM with a fine-tuned open-weight large language model developed in recent accounting research and with several tree-based models. TabFM is more accurate than all comparison models. It is also faster and less computationally intensive than the large language model. Several tree-based specifications produce predictions more quickly than TabFM, so choosing between them involves a trade-off between accuracy and speed. We conclude that TFMs have promise as a new tool for forecasting in accounting and finance. However, our evaluation is based on a single benchmark task, and no class of models is likely to dominate in all settings.

title: How Post-Training Influences Verbalized Algorithmic Computation in Language Models
summary: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from internal activations with similar accuracy in SFT and RLVR, although manipulating this information does not reliably control model outputs. In contrast, the usefulness of verbalized reasoning differs: CoTs produced by RLVR yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than those produced by SFT or DPO. We also show that carry-related statements receive higher importance scores after RLVR than matched random controls. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements but without comparable accuracy gains. These results suggest that post-training changes the usefulness of written reasoning and sensitivity to its content in meaningful ways, although greater sensitivity does not necessarily coincide with better problem performance.

title: Navigating relational agency in AI feedback musicianship: a diffractive dialogue
summary: Musical AI systems behave in non-linear, dynamic ways that exceed the tool-oriented framings inherited from earlier instrument design. Existing frames of control and ensemble interaction do not articulate the entangled, relational agency that emerges when performers work with AI feedback instruments over time. We examine a duet practice with two AI-enabled feedback instruments, Sù and Agentier, in which feedback operates at the inner level of the AI's recurrent processes and the outer loop of musical interaction between performer, instrument, and co-performer. Our work draws on agential realism and a diffractive dialogue methodology to read our independent reflections through one another across five performances, examining how agency is enacted between performers and AI instruments. We find that control and agency are relational and shift across performances; musical textures enact feedback moments of control with performers; reaching a productive feedback environment is itself a shared exploratory act; and performers maintain their instruments through funnelling and injection, developing the skill of navigating agency along a continuous spectrum. Feedback musicianship with AI instruments demands navigation of this relational agency, displacing the leading-versus-responding binary that initially framed our reflections. This work contributes a materially-grounded vocabulary for AI feedback musicianship and a model of human-AI creative collaboration in which mutual agency is worked for through practice rather than designed in.

title: Incremental Input-to-State Stabilization of Partially Unknown Control-Affine Systems within Prescribed Safe Sets
summary: Incremental input-to-state stability ($δ$-ISS) guarantees that the trajectories of a system converge towards one another, up to a gain on the difference of their inputs. Some existing learning-based designs that combine incremental stability with safety achieve only incremental input-to-state practical stability, whose non-vanishing offset can make the guarantee conservative. We consider control-affine systems with a known, full-row-rank input matrix and an unknown drift learned using Gaussian process regression. The prescribed safe set is a superlevel set of a smooth function satisfying a radial condition that ensures a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^n$ and it need not contain any equilibrium of the uncontrolled system. Using this transformation, we design a smooth feedback law and derive sufficient conditions that, under the stated learning assumptions, guarantee with high probability both forward invariance of a compact subset of the safe set and $δ$-ISS on that subset. The incremental estimate uses the distance induced by the transformation and contains no practical offset. Simulations on a Van der Pol oscillator and a Lotka-Volterra system illustrate the proposed approach.

title: Darmok: Championship Cryptic Crossword Solving via Constraint Tightening and Resilient Orchestration
summary:
We present Darmok, the first automated system to reach superhuman performance on British cryptic crosswords. Unlike American-style crosswords, cryptic clues disguise an unmarked definition and compositional wordplay beneath a misleading surface reading, sparse grids leave nearly half of each word's letters unchecked, and tournament rules rank a grid with even a single wrong or blank square behind all error-free solutions regardless of speed. Competing alongside an elite human field at the 55th Times Crossword Championship in London, Darmok solved all seven championship puzzles error-free and finished faster than every human competitor in every round. It solved the Final puzzle in 6m 52s, a full 3m 13s ahead of the human champion.
  Today's frontier AI models can on average solve a whole puzzle in a single try with comparable accuracy and speed. However, cloud API calls still stall, time out, trigger safety refusals, or get stuck in reasoning loops. To simultaneously achieve tournament-grade accuracy, speed, and reliability, Darmok cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds; uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues; and uses a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups to fill any remaining gaps without overwriting confirmed words. This design maintained near-zero-error performance across a five-month daily evaluation period. Under normal benchmark conditions, removing backup models, fallback steps, or elaborate prompt instructions barely changes accuracy, making the architecture appear over-engineered. Yet during both the worst days of daily operation and a severe slowdown of our primary model in the live Championship Final, the backup paths carried the solve, showing that as foundation models master the average case, the central challenge in building complex AI systems shifts to resilience in the worst case.

title: An Accurate Modulation-Assisted Method for Phasor Estimation Under Decaying DC Offsets
comments: This work has been submitted to the IEEE TPWRD for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Decaying DC (DDC) offsets severely compromise the accurate estimation of current phasors immediately following power grid fault occurrence. Consequently, conventional full-cycle discrete Fourier transform (FCDFT) algorithms experience decaying oscillatory magnitude errors, potentially causing distance relays to malfunction. This paper introduces a modulation-assisted technique designed to precisely eliminate the DDC components from fault current signals. By multiplying the fault signal with a high-frequency carrier and applying consecutive sliding Fourier projections, the proposed method effectively isolates the DDC signal while entirely rejecting higher-order harmonic interference. It utilizes a direct algebraic solution derived from a robust forward-difference operation across just three sequential projections to estimate and extract the DDC parameters. Furthermore, the algorithm seamlessly processes both single and multiple DDC components by dynamically tracking them as one equivalent first-order mode. Extensive evaluations are conducted to validate the proposed method accuracy. The proposed algorithm limits the maximum overshoot (MO) to 0.62% (0.59% for $k \geq 8$) for the evaluated DDC cases, and to 2.47% (0.95% at 20 dB for $k = 8$) under noisy conditions.

title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
comments: 59 pages (10 pages of main text), 18 figures, 27 tables. Code: https://github.com/vicky157/grpo-validation
summary: RLVR trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it. Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in our setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens. We introduce a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects. Across 1,668 runs on six models, matching compute reverses the ranking. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even with as much training time. A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect. In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B. These gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests. Both gains come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them. We argue that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.

title: Discovering Structurally Plausible and Interpretable Cognitive Models with Large Language Models
summary: Computational cognitive modeling has traditionally relied on manual model construction, which is a time-intensive process that requires substantial domain expertise. Although recent LLM-based approaches have begun to automate model generation, they often prioritize predictive accuracy at the expense of structural plausibility and parameter identifiability. We introduce DisCo, an LLM-guided framework that discovers interpretable symbolic cognitive models through evolutionary search with two structural components: a Validator that filters structurally invalid models, and a Cleaner that promotes parameter identifiability by removing redundant parameters. Across three behavioral tasks, DisCo consistently discovers models that achieve performance competitive with task-specific baselines. Ablation analyses show that the Validator is important for recovering psychologically meaningful structure. Without this component, models tend to violate behavioral constraints and show less consistent associations with external cognitive measures. These results suggest that LLM-driven model discovery, when coupled with appropriate structural constraints, can yield cognitively plausible models that go beyond predictive fit.

title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
comments: 25 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Zhiqun Zhao, Xiaodong Yang and Bruce Gu contributed equally. Corresponding authors: Zheng Wang, Haiquan Lu and Xiaoming Wu
summary: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.

title: Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on Edge NPUs: From NPU Only to End-to-End Performance. Extended technical report
summary: Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this methodology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves both accuracy and Runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU--workload combinations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combinations but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level performance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-E2E provides an additional 10.4--70.7\% reduction in System-level latency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-transformation and full deployment levels when comparing heterogeneous commercial Edge NPU platforms in practice.

title: A Concept-Based Interpretable Framework for Clinical Text-based Prediction via Token-Concept Attention without Concept Supervision
summary: Objective: Concept-based interpretation has emerged as a promising approach for explaining blackbox models using human-understandable, high-level concepts. However, most existing methods require annotated concept labels to train the model to identify concepts in the input, and obtaining such annotations in clinical text is often expensive. This study aims to enable concept-based interpretation for language models without concept supervision on clinical prediction tasks. Methods: We propose a novel framework that enables concept-based interpretation without concept supervision through a tailored cross-attention bottleneck. Clinical text and the text descriptions of medical concepts are first tokenized and embedded by a pretrained language model. A cross-attention module then estimates the presence of each concept for each text token, producing concept relevance scores that capture how concepts are involved throughout the note. These scores are pooled and used in a linear prediction layer to model clinical outcomes in an interpretable manner. Results: The performance of the proposed framework was compared against blackbox models across two tasks: chest trauma severity stratification using a private dataset and an in-hospital mortality prediction task using the publicly available MIMIC-III dataset. The proposed framework achieved AUROC values within 0.02 of the corresponding blackbox models. The framework also enabled cohort- and patient-level interpretation, capturing the overall concept importance across the cohort and patient-specific concept contributions. Conclusion: Our proposed framework realizes concept-based interpretation without requiring ground-truth concept presence labels. It improves the transparency of clinical text predictions while maintaining strong performance in clinical prediction tasks.

title: Investigating Composite Modeling in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Design
summary: Scientific design often requires balancing competing objectives that are expensive to evaluate through experiments or simulations. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) addresses this challenge by using probabilistic models to guide the selection of promising designs. In many applications, tunable inputs map to observable intermediate responses, which are then combined through known functions to compute the final objectives. Prior work on Bayesian optimization of composite functions shows that learning from these intermediate responses, which we call Composite modeling, can substantially improve sampling efficiency in single-objective optimization, compared to methods that condition only on black-box observations of the objective function. The benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO, however, remain understudied. In this work, we study the benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO and investigate the factors driving variation in its gains. We first establish single-objective conditions under which intermediate observations provide no additional predictive information beyond objective values, where composite and black box methods use the same warped Gaussian process prior. Controlled numerical experiments with versions of four MOBO methods across eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific-design benchmarks examine how these conditions relate to optimization gains in the multi-objective setting, where the black box approach models the objective functions with a standard multi-output Gaussian process. Both investigations support the claim that composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine.

title: Metamorphic testing of learned AC optimal power flow surrogates reveals representation dependence
comments: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshops on (i) Trustworthy AI Evaluation, (ii) AI Foundations for Power Grids, (iii) Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning, (iv) Sim2Science, and (v) Representations for the Physical Sciences
summary: Evaluating a learned AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF) surrogate on one grid serialization cannot show whether its accuracy depends on that encoding. We test this dependence with thirteen metamorphic relations, each specifying when a transformation is valid and how to compare its outputs. Our audit covers 17 model and pipeline configurations: two released trained checkpoints and 15 random-weight architecture or mechanism controls. Every configuration violates at least six relations, even at reporting tolerances ten times tighter or looser. For GridSFM-Open v1.1, source inspection and intermediate-tensor interventions point to an indexing bug and three noncanonical or numerically unstable preprocessing choices; a repaired checkpoint remains untested. In a separate case500 training experiment, augmentation lowers transformed-view error in three of four models and median discrepancy and constraint-violation P95 in all four. These benefits depend on the training protocol: some relations worsen, and every evaluated prediction remains AC infeasible. A GPU/CPU eigensolver mismatch accounts for most of the large raw-Laplacian-baseline gain. We recommend reporting representation consistency alongside accuracy, feasibility, and cost. These results establish neither deployment readiness nor universal invariance.

title: Pair-Merge Tokenisation Is Hard to Approximate on Binary Strings and Strongly NP-Hard on Unary Datasets
comments: 34 pages, 11 figures. Code and certificates: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24023730
summary: Tokenisers such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) shorten text by repeatedly merging an adjacent pair of symbols into a new one; fewer tokens mean less computation. We ask whether an efficient algorithm can choose $k$ merges that leave a string of length $n$ almost as short as possible; doing nothing is already within a factor $n$. We prove that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm comes within a factor $c\,n/\log n$, for some constant $c>0$, already for one binary string and for BPE-style merges that replace every occurrence. The key idea is that $k$ merges form a grammar with $k$ rules: a vertex-cover gap becomes a grammar-size gap, which we amplify with relabelled copies, encode in binary and realise with explicit merges. For merges that may skip occurrences, a simple algorithm achieves $O(n/\log\log n)$, and no Karp reduction can prove hardness beyond order $n/\log n$ unless coNP $\subseteq$ NP/poly. Over a one-letter alphabet, both tokenisation problems left open by Kastreva et al. are strongly NP-complete on datasets with repeated strings.
comment: 34 pages, 11 figures. Code and certificates: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24023730

title: Improved Bounds for Online Matching with Random Edge Arrivals
summary: We study the unweighted online matching problem with random edge arrivals, where each edge arrives at an independent time drawn uniformly from $[0,1]$, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject it while maintaining a matching. Guruganesh and Singla (IPCO, 2017) first broke the $1/2$ barrier of the naive Greedy algorithm by giving a $(1/2+\varepsilon)$-competitive algorithm for a small constant $\varepsilon>0$, a guarantee that has remained the best known for nearly a decade. We give a simple three-phase algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of $0.5445$ by deliberately rejecting selected early edges to reserve their endpoints for later matching opportunities. With a different choice of parameters, the same algorithm is $0.5535$-competitive on triangle-free graphs, including bipartite graphs. We also establish competitive ratio upper bounds below $0.6964$ for general graphs and $0.7043$ for bipartite graphs via exact rational evaluation of an optimal-policy recurrence on fixed graphs, even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism.

title: Market-Conditioned JEPA: Learning from Unpredictable Market Shocks
summary: Much of the variation in financial time series is driven by market-wide shocks that cannot be predicted from an asset's own history. Per-asset self-supervised learning treats this variation as irreducible noise. Under a latent factor model, we show that conditioning prediction on the realized market factor makes the asset's market exposure necessary for optimal prediction, while reducing the noise against which the asset-specific component is learned. Building on this insight, we introduce Market-Conditioned JEPA (MC-JEPA), a joint-embedding predictive architecture for financial time series. During training, we construct a leave-one-out market condition for each asset from the future target embeddings of other assets and incorporate it through factor loadings derived from the asset's own representation. On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data, MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA across nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, with the strongest and most statistically significant gains in exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the best RankIC on all liquidity targets and on return horizons from two hours to five days, outperforming time-series foundation models and self-supervised baselines, and delivers the best portfolio performance in a historical backtest. Ablations show that the return and exposure gains require the condition to be aligned with the realized market movement. After restoring the volatility scale removed by normalization, the predictor's factor loadings rank stocks by market beta nearly as well as a supervised probe, without labels. A synthetic factor-model study with known parameters shows that conditioning improves the recovery of both market exposure and the asset-specific component.

title: Third-Order Asymptotics for Fixed-Length Lossy Compression of Discrete Memoryless Sources
summary: This paper determines the third-order asymptotics of the logarithm of the minimum codebook size for fixed-length lossy compression of discrete memoryless sources. For an excess-distortion probability constraint $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and every interior distortion level, we establish a third-order correction of $\frac12\log n+O(1)$, where $n$ is the blocklength. This sharpens the general bounds of Kostina and Verdú [IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory, 2012]. The main technical innovation lies in the converse for positive dispersion. Under a reverse change of measure, we retain the exponential weights associated with tilted information and distortion slack and control them jointly using the multivariate weighted-strip estimate of Scarlett, Martinez, and Guillén i Fàbregas [Proc. IEEE ISIT, 2015]. A pairing argument verifies the required covariance nondegeneracy uniformly over all reconstruction words whose distortion balls meet a typical set, yielding the matching converse.

title: Greedy+Singleton for knapsack-constrained monotone submodular maximization has approximation ratio exactly $β^\star \approx 0.42944$
comments: 26 pages, 4 figures. Code and certificates: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24023723
summary: Greedy+Singleton is the textbook heuristic for monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint: it returns the better of the cost-benefit greedy set and the best single item. Its worst-case approximation ratio, known only to lie in $[0.427, 0.42945]$ (Feldman-Nutov-Shoham; Kulik-Schwartz-Shachnai), is exactly an explicit constant $β^\star\approx 0.42944$. In the extremal instances, many cheap "filler" items wear down the value of two large optimal items while greedy spends the budget, until neither fits. This picture gives a sharper factor-revealing relaxation; we bound it analytically near the extremal parameters, up to finitely many interval-arithmetic checks, and certify it elsewhere by an exact branch-and-bound. The matching bad instances are tie-free and checkable by hand. For the version that stops at the first item that does not fit, Wolsey's bound $1-e^{-β_W}\approx 0.35780$, where $e^{β_W}=2-β_W$, is tight; Wolsey stated this for his variant without giving the instances, and we give an explicit family with no ties that also covers comparison with the best feasible singleton. The CELF rule also has ratio exactly $β^\star$.
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures. Code and certificates: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24023723

title: PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation
summary: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.

title: TERM: Target-Free Jailbreak Defense via Entropy-Guided Residual Modulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

title: Lightweight Deep Learning Framework for Astrocyte-Centric 3D Reconstruction across Normal and Stress-associated Ultrastructural States
comments: Accepted for publication in npj Imaging. 19 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables, including Supplementary Material. Code is available at https://github.com/QuIN-Lab/AstroSeg-vEM
summary: The morphology of astrocytes is closely associated with their ability to support and modulate neural circuit functions; however, its reconstruction from volume electron microscopy (vEM) data remains labor-intensive and computationally resource-intensive, placing substantial barriers on its broader adoption and scalability despite the high spatial resolution of vEM. We present AstroSeg-vEM, a lightweight, astrocyte-centric framework for morphology-preserving astrocyte segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and quantitative morphological analysis in vEM images. AstroSeg-vEM combines transformer-based 2D segmentation with dedicated post-processing methods and operates directly on high-resolution EM sections, making it well suited to anisotropic vEM data and downstream proofreading workflows while preserving the full in-plane resolution of the original EM data. Across four mouse hippocampal datasets representing normal and morphologically defined stress-associated astrocyte ultrastructural states, AstroSeg-vEM demonstrates robust performance and generalization, achieving average Dice and weighted Dice values of 0.92 and 0.95, respectively, on a held-out test dataset. Its lightweight architecture enables efficient, high-fidelity reconstruction on consumer-grade hardware, providing a scalable and accessible platform for large-scale astrocyte ultrastructure analysis and future astrocyte-neuron interaction studies.

title: Approximating graphic TSP by b-matchings
summary: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for graphic TSP that returns a tour of length at most $\frac{89}{64}=\frac{7}{5}-\frac{3}{320}$ times the value of the subtour relaxation. This improves the long-standing ratio $\frac75$ of Sebő and Vygen and shows that the integrality gap of the subtour LP on graphic instances is at most $\frac{89}{64}\approx 1.3906$. We optimize a non-linear objective function over an odd-join polytope, which uses (i) a new removable system of edges, and (ii) reconnection of subtours if the graph is disconnected. This approach gives a $\frac{13}{10}$-approximation algorithm for $4$-regular $4$-vertex-connected graphs, improving the $\frac43$ of Newman, and a $\frac43$-approximation for $k$-vertex-connected graphs of maximum degree at most $k+1$, for every $k\ge 3$. For the general graphic TSP, we construct a feasible point in the odd-join polytope, using an optimal vertex from the Subtour linear programming relaxation of TSP, which helps us bound the approximation factor by 89/64.

title: Two nodally bound-preserving and mass-conservative discontinuous Galerkin methods for reaction-diffusion problems
summary: We propose and analyze two high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods that preserve prescribed nodal bounds and total mass for reaction-diffusion problems with anisotropic and heterogeneous diffusion. Both methods combine a weighted interior-penalty prediction step with a convex correction in either the dG energy or the $L^2$ metric. We construct a pointwise bound-preserving and cellwise mass-preserving comparison function with optimal local approximation properties. This construction yields optimal dG-energy error estimates for the energy correction and, under a dual regularity assumption, optimal $L^2$ and dG-energy error estimates for the $L^2$ correction on quasi-uniform meshes. We further establish a general a posteriori estimate that combines a predictor estimator with the computable correction norm. The resulting estimators are globally reliable and efficient up to data oscillation, with parameter-dependent efficiency constants. Numerical experiments compare the two corrections and illustrate their use in adaptive computations.

title: Few-Shot Residual Adaptation of Pretrained Latent World Models
summary: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.

title: Transformers Provably Learn Graph Search: Training Dynamics and the Exponential Power of Depth
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. We first characterize the architectural requirements for this task, proving that one-layer transformers require $Ω(N^2)$ size on dense graphs to implement the key DFS child-selection primitive. While a two-layer transformer implements full DFS with $O(N\log(N))$ size. Thus, a second layer is necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning. We then extend this expressivity analysis to deeper models: for every $k\geq3$, a $k$-layer transformer implements a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon $1+2^{k-3}$, establishing an exponential increase in reachability horizon with depth. Finally, going beyond expressivity, given appropriately curated training data, we show that two-layer transformers can provably learn to execute DFS via gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs. Together, our results provide a mechanistic account of how transformers implement graph search, how depth expands bounded look-ahead, and how such reasoning algorithms can emerge through training.

title: IFRS Compliance Verification: An Open Multi-LLM Benchmark and Content-Conditioned Ensemble Classifier
summary: Verifying corporate financial disclosures against the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is a core auditing task in which experts cross-reference disclosures with hundreds of fine-grained regulatory paragraphs: a laborious, costly, and error-prone process that motivates growing interest in large language models (LLMs) as compliance assistants. Yet single-model accuracy remains insufficient for high-stakes use, and naive ensembling is vulnerable to systematic per-model biases that can drag aggregate accuracy below that of the strongest individual annotator. This gap is addressed with a multi-stage framework, supported by a new benchmark of 19,998 IFRS regulation-disclosure pairs comprising 11,161 unanimous multi-LLM labels and 8,837 human annotations on items where the LLMs disagreed. The framework couples a three-stage domain-adapted sentence embedding pipeline (BERT masked language modeling on SEC EDGAR filings, unsupervised TSDAE and SimCSE adaptation, and supervised contrastive alignment) with a learned ensemble classifier that fuses frozen embeddings and LLM probability features from GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro via Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) optimized gradient-boosted trees. On the disagreement set, the ensemble achieves 81.7% weighted F1, exceeding the strongest single LLM by 10.4 points and majority voting by 14.6 points, and outperforms eleven unsupervised aggregation baselines; the retrieval pipeline attains Recall@15 of 45.3% on unseen regulations. The dataset, model checkpoints, annotation platform, and classifier implementation will be publicly released.

title: Towards Reliable VLM Judges: State-Conditional Invariance and Presentation-Aware Diagnostics
comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets). 47 pages, 16 figures. Project page: https://xinyuw922-pixel.github.io/Towards-Reliable-VLM-Judge/ ; Code: https://github.com/xinyuw922-pixel/Towards-Reliable-VLM-Judge ; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/nahco318/Towards-Reliable-VLM-Judges
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.

title: Compute the Interactions, Not the Attributes: What a Fact Layer Must Supply in the Chinese Sexagenary System
summary: Language-model systems in rule-governed domains often pair the model with a deterministic fact layer, but which facts that layer should supply is rarely measured. We measure it in the Chinese sexagenary system underlying BaZi chart analysis, where every fact has one table-checkable value: 682 items over twelve fact categories and 160 transit--natal collision items, posed closed-book, with the reference table, and with computed facts at increasing levels. In eleven open-weight models answering directly, errors concentrate where attributes must be combined: none gets more than 4\% of sexagenary days or 1\% of collisions right. Static attributes have no consistent effect, and the complete relation list leaves most direct-answering models near zero although it contains the answer. A query-filtered layer (exploratory) raises Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B to 78--92\% and four further models to 96--100\%. Three proprietary reasoning models compute 68--95\% of collisions unaided. On chess positions, under predictions locked in advance, attributes again do not substitute for relations and listed distractors are misattributed. The fact layer must supply computed interactions; how they are presented depends on the model and the domain.

title: Unified Optimization of Traffic Signal and Lane Channelization for an Isolated Intersection Using Reinforcement Learning
summary: Optimizing traffic signal control has been a long-lasting critical issue in traffic engineering, and a number of robust methodologies have emerged to solve the problem so far. On the other hand, the road design for lane channelization is a static problem that is difficult to solve jointly with the real-time traffic signal control. If traffic volume does not vary, it is possible that both problems can be solved in an integrated manner as a single static optimization problem. Recently, researchers have devised a mixed integer linear problem (MILP) to jointly determine the traffic signal and road width designs. However, this joint optimization problem must be solved repeatedly whenever the traffic flow pattern varies. Solving the MILP may also take impractical computing time as the problem size gets larger. We present a robust methodology for solving the joint optimization problem using reinforcement learning (RL) on a real-time basis. Abrupt changes in lane markings with an incompatible signal phase can jeopardize drivers. To sidestep such a dangerous action change, we train a model with human feedback to filter infeasible action transitions in a rule-based manner. We devised a deep Q-network that can accommodate joint actions for traffic signal and lane marking plans. To ensure the implementation of the proposed operation, a variable sign for lane markings is necessary at each stop line of an intersection. The experimental results confirm that the proposed methodology enhances the intersection performance by increasing throughput.

title: Parameterized Complexity and Geometric Approximation of Riesz Energy Subset Selection
comments: 35 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, and instructions for reproducing the experiments: https://github.com/emmerichmtm/PCGA-Riesz
summary: We choose $k$ of $n$ sites to minimize Riesz $s$-energy, in which a pair at distance $t$ contributes $t^{-s}$. For $s=2$, exact selection is polynomial on a line but NP-hard in the plane. Adapting the proxy lemma of Ceccarello et al. gives an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (EPAS) for fixed Euclidean dimension and fixed $s>0$. To sharpen the bound, we start with a geometric packing. Farthest-first traversal gives $2k$ centers separated by at least the last insertion distance $r$. If one site of an optimum is removed, each of the $k-1$ remaining sites excludes at most one center closer than $r/2$, leaving at least $k+1$ centers free. The new step is a discrete exchange bound: the removed site's interaction energy is at most the average it would contribute at those free centers. In the plane at $s=2$, this reduces the representative bound from $O(k^2\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$ for a packing estimate of total energy to $O(k\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$, independently of $n$. Rational planar examples show that the resulting separation scale $r/\sqrt{\log(2k)}$ is sharp. A $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation on rational planar sites takes $O(nk+n\log n)+(C\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)^k$ operations of polynomial bit cost. The observed number $M$ of representatives determines the search size $\binom{M}{k}$. With one million sites, $k=5$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$, the exchange grid left 252 subsets on clustered inputs and about $9.3\times10^{26}$ on uniform inputs. The method extends to metrics of bounded doubling dimension and to compact domains with effective geometric routines, including filled simple polygons. At $s=2$, exact decision on metrics with nonzero distances in $\{1,2\}$ is W[1]-complete in $k$. A gap that shrinks with $k$ rules out a deterministic EPAS on unrestricted metrics unless FPT = W[1].

title: One Byte, One Token: Byteifying a 27B Hybrid-Attention LLM with Self-Generated Data
comments: Full text in English followed by the full text in Chinese. 39 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and task suite: https://huggingface.co/datasets/leiwhere/ld3-byte-eval
summary: Byte-level BPE fragments Chinese text (for Qwen3.8 on Chinese Wikipedia, 3.84 bytes per token on average; 64% of tokens are single characters) and hides spelling from the model. We ask whether an already-trained 27B subword model can be converted directly into a pure byte-level model (one byte, one token), without a patching structure or a local encoder, while keeping most of its ability. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B (48 Gated DeltaNet layers + 16 full-attention layers), we shrink the vocabulary from 248,320 to 384 entries (the 256 byte symbols already in the BPE vocabulary plus special ids), leave every other weight untouched, and continue training in a two-stage curriculum (encoding first, then reading) on 4.77 GB of supervised bytes: all dialogue/behavioral supervision is generated on-policy by the original model itself (character dictionary, word dictionary, general dialogue, coding sessions), and knowledge reading uses encyclopedia text (54% of supervised bytes). Training takes 178.6 h on 8xH200. On the same GPU and serving stack, the byte model's gap to the original falls within the paired bootstrap interval on MATH-500, HumanEval+, MMLU-Pro and non-thinking GSM8K, and it loses 4-6 points on C-Eval, thinking-mode GSM8K and non-thinking IFEval. Without thinking it leads on every character-level task (CUTE 75.2 -> 84.0, EXECUTE-zho 81.6 -> 93.9, our Chinese character suite 54.4 -> 64.0), but lookup knowledge about Chinese characters such as pronunciation and stroke count drops, and thinking does not recover it. The cost is throughput: per-step speed is identical, but each step yields 3-5x less output; Chinese characters per second is about 1/4 of the original, and prefill at 64K bytes is 6.5x slower. We also document four byte-model failure modes (greedy runaway, sampling breaking UTF-8, ineffective penalty terms on a small vocabulary, repetition) and their fixes.

title: Post-OCR Correction of Mixed-Script Uzbek Text: Byte-Level ByT5 with an Empirical Homoglyph Noise Matrix
comments: 7 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the 10th International Conference on Future Networks and Distributed Systems (ICFNDS 2026), ACM ICPS. Code: https://github.com/OybekNarzullaev/byt5-uzbek-postocr
summary: In Uzbek official and technical documents, a large share of OCR errors is caused not by poor image quality but by characters that are visually identical across the two alphabets in use. Because the script transition is still under way, Cyrillic and Latin appear on the same page and often within a single sentence, and in our measurements the density of homoglyph errors on such pages is close to five times higher than in single-script text. We study this problem in a setting where the corpus of engineering-geological and ICT infrastructure reports may not leave the organisation, so every stage was executed on local hardware. The proposed system combines a byte-level ByT5 model with a noise generator whose sampling weights are estimated from 359 manually classified error events, together with a Levenshtein-bounded conservative decoding rule. On a Gold set of 5,204 line pairs it lowers the character error rate from 0.0578 to 0.0369, restores 91.3% of the homoglyphs and introduces only 84 new errors.

title: From Egocentric Human Video to Robot Manipulation in the Era of Embodied Intelligence
summary: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.

title: Earth Embeddings in Environmental Remote Sensing
summary: Earth observations from satellite platforms have profoundly transformed research and applications across numerous domains. However, uneven observation coverage and frequent data gaps continue to limit their ability to capture Earth's surface dynamics. Moreover, processing multi-modal Earth observations requires substantial computational resources and sophisticated data harmonization frameworks, which may not be readily accessible to many remote sensing practitioners. Earth embeddings have emerged as promising solutions to these challenges. As general-purpose representations converted from multi-source Earth observations, Earth embeddings can support a wide range of downstream tasks with no requirement of task-specific feature design and preprocessing. In this study, we first introduce the theoretical foundations of Earth embeddings. Then, we review several representative Earth embedding products. We next examine the applications of Earth embeddings across six major domains of environmental remote sensing. Finally, we systematically assess the performance of Earth embeddings in four downstream tasks, including hyperspectral image classification, individual tree crown segmentation, crop yield prediction, and aboveground biomass mapping. Our review and case studies suggest that, despite several advantages over conventional Earth observation data, current Earth embeddings do not always outperform remote sensing imagery or hand-crafted features. Earth embeddings should not be viewed as a direct replacement for conventional EO data, but rather as representations that provide stable information across space and time. Remote sensing practitioners may consider evaluating Earth embeddings' suitability for specific tasks and using them strategically, rather than assuming superior performance by default.

title: Megrez: A Knowledge-Guided Agent for Formal Mathematics over MK Set Theory
summary: General-purpose coding agents equipped with proof-assistant tools have shown strong performance on standalone competition problems, yet cumulative textbook formalization inside a low-resource mathematical library still faces three obstacles: aligning textbook concepts with library declarations, keeping long-horizon search synchronized with live proof states, and integrating locally verified proofs reliably into a growing codebase. We present Megrez, a knowledge-guided formalization agent for Rocq libraries built on Morse--Kelley (MK) set theory. Megrez coordinates a general coding agent through three mechanisms: (1) a source-rebuildable knowledge graph merging formal declarations, compiler references, and curated metadata to support retrieval via Chinese aliases, concept clusters, proof dependencies, and multi-lane full-text ranking; (2) a feedback-driven 1--5 tactic short-burst proving loop paired with a goal-local branch ledger and exponential-interval structured reflection; and (3) a three-check acceptance pipeline (statement fidelity, axiom auditing, and full builds) coupled with a multi-corpus Provider stack and a candidate-bound recoverable batch state machine. Deployment and evaluation on a point-set topology corpus demonstrate effective cross-chapter formalization and scalable premise retrieval.

title: Synapse-Control: Making Agent Experience Actionable with Lightweight Runtime Control
summary: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.

title: When to Start Denoising? Adaptive Denoising Entry for Generative Video Compression
summary: Generative video compression offers a promising solution for compressing and reconstructing videos under extremely low bitrate constraints, among which the diffusion-based solutions still achieve the best performance by providing the powerful generative latent prior. However, their effectiveness critically depends on when the compressed latent is introduced into the diffusion process, which directly governs the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. To address this limitation, we identify denoising start-timestep selection as a key factor governing this trade-off and formulate it as a geometric optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we propose a novel adaptive diffusion entry method for generative video compression (ADE-GVC), the first timestep-aware generative video compression framework, featuring a lightweight predictor that estimates an adaptive denoising start point from the compressed latent. A temporal adapter further extracts compression-aware conditions and injects them into a pretrained video diffusion model, enabling the reconstruction of videos with both high fidelity and realism. More importantly, we observe a strong quantitative relationship between the predicted timesteps and the distortion between the original and compressed latents, providing empirical support for our optimization formulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADE-GVC achieves the state-of-the-art performance on perceptual metrics and substantially improves reconstruction realism over existing generative video compression methods. Notably, our ADE-GVC achieves an average bitrate savings of 40.99\% (on DISTS) and 95.24\% (on PSNR) compared to the latest open-source baseline GLC-Video.

title: PUMA: Probability-Constrained Sequential Interaction for Forensic Localization
summary: Image manipulation localization must jointly exploit semantic structure and noise-sensitive forensic evidence. However, the effects of spatial correspondence, matching quality, and interaction order are often conflated. Existing semantic-forensic fusion methods provide complementary representations, but do not explicitly preserve quality-mismatch information during spatial correspondence or adaptively select the order in which information is propagated across branches. We propose PUMA (Probability-constrained Unbalanced Matching and Aggregation), which combines spatially constrained unbalanced optimal transport with position-wise convex selection between two sequential operators through a shared positional interface. Before normalization, PUMA retains signed transport-mass residuals, constructs row-stochastic cross-branch and within-noise-branch operators, and updates noise features through a gated residual path. PUMA achieves strong localization results on four test sets, with scores on COVERAGE and NIST16 exceeding the published results of the representative methods listed in our comparison. The experiments support the utility of local matching states and adaptive sequential interaction for cross-source localization and several post-processing conditions.

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity
summary: Many-query analyses, in which a computational model is repeatedly evaluated, play an important role in uncertainty quantification and optimization for engineering design. However, many-query analyses can be prohibitively expensive when considering high-fidelity numerical models, especially those governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Surrogate modeling replaces costly simulations with cheap approximations, enabling practical uncertainty quantification and design workflows. Machine learning (ML) approaches to surrogate modeling have gained significant traction in the development of surrogate models due to their non-intrusive nature; they do not require access to the underlying simulation code. The Operator Inference (OpInf) approach, in particular, fits reduced operators to state and corresponding time derivative data. However, high-fidelity training data is scarce due to limited computational budgets, and OpInf models trained on such scarce data often exhibit high variance, a critical liability in high-risk engineering design. We propose Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), which reduces this variance by supplementing scarce high-fidelity snapshots with abundant low-fidelity data drawn from coarser discretizations of the same problem. MF-OpInf handles data across varying fidelity levels by utilizing a multifidelity linear regression framework to estimate the reduced operators. Numerical experiments on model PDE problems demonstrate that MF-OpInf predicts PDE solution fields with higher accuracy compared to the high-fidelity-only OpInf with the same computational budget.

title: FlashMotion: Ultra-Fast Long-Term 3D Motion Generation
summary: 3D human motion generation plays a crucial role in game development, extended reality (XR), digital humans, and embodied simulation. Beyond motion generation, practical pipelines include rigging, retargeting, and rendering, making ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation without compromising quality valuable for real-time interactive applications. Despite promising progress, high-quality long-horizon motion generation under tight inference budgets remains challenging, owing to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget, covering text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture tasks. To enhance trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, together with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlashMotion achieves overall state-of-the-art performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation. Code is available at FlashMotion (https://github.com/Sun-Happy-YKX/FlashMotion).

title: Curriculum proof repair with learned counterexamples
summary: Language models (LMs) have substantially lowered the barrier to applying formal verification for building reliable and secure software. Existing approaches commonly follow the verifier-in-the-loop paradigm, but the verifier often provides only coarse, binary pass/fail feedback, which offers little actionable signal on how the proof should be repaired. Recent work shows that counterexamples provide more actionable feedback by grounding proof failures in concrete program states, but generating useful ones at inference time requires costly iterative refinement. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based framework for Verus proof repair that internalizes counterexample-guided diagnosis as a model capability, producing useful counterexamples in a single pass. Our key insight is to train counterexample generation not as a standalone validation task, but as a data-driven diagnostic objective: a counterexample is useful when conditioning on it helps the model produce a safe, verifier-passing proof. Given a failed Verus proof and verifier error, TopoVerus generates a structured source-level counterexample, repair rationale, and repaired proof in one trajectory, optimized with reinforcement learning from Verus feedback and a proof-code safety gate. To guide the order of invariant repairs, TopoVerus introduces a curriculum with a topological graph reward based on invariant dependencies derived from inductiveness tests, which encourages counterexample generation to follow the same topological order. Across seven Verus benchmarks with 471 problems, TopoVerus achieves 61.6%/72.2% weighted-average Safe-Pass@1/Safe-Pass@3, outperforming the strongest baseline, Claude Sonnet 4.5, by 5.7/6.3 points. We also show that TopoVerus's learned counterexamples can directly augment the reasoning of existing LM-based proof repair approaches, improving their success rate by 64.3% compared to chain-of-thought diagnostics.

title: DepthGS: Depth-Guided Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Regularization for High-Quality Surface Reconstruction
comments: To appear in IEEE Trans. on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
summary: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently explored, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To fill the above gap, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view settings, and rigorously establish corresponding upper bounds on reconstruction error. The above analysis informs the design of adaptive regularization strategies in both single-view and multi-view optimization. More specifically, for single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. For multi-view optimization, we introduce a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that promotes consistency between neighboring-view depth maps and the corresponding depth predictions obtained by transforming the current view's depth predictions into those neighboring views. Extensive experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis.
comment: To appear in IEEE Trans. on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence

title: An IoT Based Approach for Platform Independent Positioning Service
summary: KAIST Indoor Localization System (KAILOS) was introduced in 2014 and became one of the world-first complete indoor positioning solutions. It is mainly based on the WiFi signal to estimate location and provide positioning service via mobile application that has many restrictions by the Operating System. This study proposes an extended architecture of KAILOS to make use of the IoT device for removing the barriers of the mobile-app-based approach and conveniently providing indoor positioning service. Design of the IoT device that contains hardware and software is also presented. Via this study, we prove that the IoT-based approach is promising and can be a crucial feature to widen applications of indoor localization services.

title: Min-CSPs on Complete Instances III: Nearly Optimal Characterizations of Approximation for Symmetric CSPs
summary:
This paper studies complete Min-$k$-CSPs: an instance on $n$ variables has one nontrivial constraint for every $k$-set of variables (so $\binom{n}{k}$ constraints in total), and the goal is to find an assignment that minimizes the number of unsatisfied constraints. They are motivated by the connections to machine learning and data science, as well as the possibility of being testbeds for new algorithmic techniques. Previous recent results presented polynomial-time algorithms for the decision version of every complete Boolean $k$-CSP, which is a necessary condition for any multiplicative approximations for the minimization version, but nontrivial approximation results have been limited to fragile CSPs, 2-SAT, and NAE-3-SAT, leaving the approximability of most complete Boolean Min-CSPs open, including complete Min-$k$-SAT.
  In this paper, we resolve this question, up to nearly matching factors, for the natural class of symmetric Boolean predicates. Given $A \subseteq \{0, \dots, k\}$, Min-CSP($A$) is a Min-$k$-CSP where each constraint is specified by $k$ literals and is satisfied if the number of true literals belongs to $A$. Let $w(A)$ be the maximum number of consecutive integers in $A$. Our main results for complete Min-CSP($A$) are (1) a QPTAS for $w(A) \leq 2$ and (2) an $\widetilde{O}(n^{w(A)-3})$-approximation for $w(A) \geq 3$, as well as almost matching hardness results for the latter. Our QPTAS for $w(A)=2$ significantly improves the previous $O(1)$-approximation for Min-2-SAT and the $\operatorname{polylog}(n)$-approximation for Min-NAE-3-SAT, as well as extends the PTAS for fragile CSPs (i.e., $w(A) = 1$).

title: An Interpretable Stylometric Framework for Early Chinese Buddhist Translator Styles: A Case Study on the Attribution of Disputed Works of An Shigao
comments: Presented as a long paper at Digital Humanities 2026 (DH2026) in Daejeon, Republic of Korea. The abstract appears DH2026 Book of Abstracts, pp. 545-549, available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22656106
summary: Attributing early Chinese Buddhist translations requires evidence that scholars can trace back to the texts. We develop an interpretable stylometric framework that uses features defined or reviewed by Buddhist philologists, including function characters, sentence formulas, sentence-final characters, sentence length, and part-of-speech n-grams. We construct stylistic profiles from 31 authenticated translations by seven translators from the Eastern Han through the Western Jin, then compare eight disputed texts with An Shigao's profile. Two texts, T1557 and T0101, show the strongest stylistic similarity to the authenticated An Shigao corpus, with scores of 0.783 and 0.687, respectively. The attributions agree with those reported by a published BERT-based approach on the same set of disputed texts. The framework requires no task-specific training and allows scholars to inspect which linguistic features support each proposed attribution.

title: picoEmergencyNet : Attention-Enhanced Ultra-Small Deep Learning Model for Aerial Image Classification in Emergency Monitoring
comments: 6 pages, Appeared in IJCNN2026 C. Kyrkou, "picoEmergencyNet: Attention-Enhanced Ultra-Small Deep Learning Model for Aerial Image Classification in Emergency Monitoring," 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), Maastricht, Netherlands, 2026, pp. 1-6
summary: Real-time disaster recognition from aerial imagery requires deep learning models that operate under strict memory, compute, and latency constraints. While recent approaches achieve high accuracy, their computational cost limits deployment on resource-constrained UAV platforms. This work introduces picoEmergencyNet, an ultra-lightweight convolutional neural network designed for aerial image disaster classification. The proposed architecture combines depthwise dilated convolutions with efficient channel attention and channel shuffling to enable multi-scale feature extraction at minimal computational cost. picoEmergencyNet has 23k parameters and 7M FLOPs, requiring only 0.1 MB of model storage. Evaluated on the AIDER and AIDERv2 disaster datasets, it achieves up to 96.1% accuracy, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art lightweight models that are orders of magnitude larger. Deployment experiments on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin show that, without hardware-specific optimizations, picoEmergencyNet achieves 258 FPS on GPU and 46 FPS on CPU with a 7x lower activation memory footprint compared to competing models. These results demonstrate that careful architectural specialization, rather than model scaling, enables highly efficient and accurate TinyML-ready disaster recognition for real-time UAV-based emergency monitoring.
