title: MDS Array Codes With Small Sub-packetization Levels and Small Repair Degrees
comments: Accepted for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory
summary: High-rate minimum storage regenerating (MSR) codes are known to require a large sub-packetization level, which can make meta-data management difficult and hinder implementation in practical systems. A few maximum distance separable (MDS) array code constructions have been proposed to attain a much smaller sub-packetization level by sacrificing a bit of repair bandwidth. However, to the best of our knowledge, only one construction by Guruswami et al. can support the repair of a failed node without contacting all the surviving nodes. This construction is certainly of theoretical interest but not yet practical due to its requirement for very large code parameters. In this paper, we propose a generic transformation that can convert any $(\overline{n}, \overline{k})$ MSR code with a repair degree of $\overline{d}<\overline{n}-1$ into another $(n=s\overline{n},k)$ MDS array code that supports $d<n-1$ with a small sub-packetization level and $(1+ε)$-optimal repair bandwidth (i.e., $1+ε$ times the optimal value) under a specific condition. We obtain three MDS array codes with small sub-packetization levels and $(1+ε)$-optimal repair bandwidth by applying this transformation to three known MSR codes. All the new MDS array codes have a small repair degree of $d<n-1$ and work for both small and large code parameters.
comment: Accepted for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory

title: Linear-time Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding with Reference Aggregation
comments: ACL 2024. v3: More accurate time measurements for ChrF
summary: Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding is a text generation technique that has been shown to improve the quality of machine translations, but is expensive, even if a sampling-based approximation is used. Besides requiring a large number of sampled sequences, it requires the pairwise calculation of a utility metric, which has quadratic complexity. In this paper, we propose to approximate pairwise metric scores with scores calculated against aggregated reference representations. This changes the complexity of utility estimation from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$, while empirically preserving most of the quality gains of MBR decoding. We release our source code at https://github.com/ZurichNLP/mbr
comment: ACL 2024. v3: More accurate time measurements for ChrF

title: Bandit Profit-maximization for Targeted Marketing
comments: The Twenty-Fifth ACM Conference on Economics and Computation (EC'24). v3 corrects minor errors in the published version
summary:
We study a sequential profit-maximization problem, optimizing for both price and ancillary variables like marketing expenditures. Specifically, we aim to maximize profit over an arbitrary sequence of multiple demand curves, each dependent on a distinct ancillary variable, but sharing the same price. A prototypical example is targeted marketing, where a firm (seller) wishes to sell a product over multiple markets. The firm may invest different marketing expenditures for different markets to optimize customer acquisition, but must maintain the same price across all markets. Moreover, markets may have heterogeneous demand curves, each responding to prices and marketing expenditures differently. The firm's objective is to maximize its gross profit, the total revenue minus marketing costs.
  Our results are near-optimal algorithms for this class of problems in an adversarial bandit setting, where demand curves are arbitrary non-adaptive sequences, and the firm observes only noisy evaluations of chosen points on the demand curves. For $n$ demand curves (markets), we prove a regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(nT^{3/4})$ and a lower bound of $Ω((nT)^{3/4})$ for monotonic demand curves, and a regret bound of $\tildeΘ(nT^{2/3})$ for demand curves that are monotonic in price and concave in the ancillary variables.
comment: The Twenty-Fifth ACM Conference on Economics and Computation (EC'24). v3 corrects minor errors in the published version

title: Robustness Verification in Neural Networks
comments: 16 pages, 1 figure, v2: corrected typo in the title
summary:
In this paper we investigate formal verification problems for Neural Network computations. Of central importance will be various robustness and minimization problems such as: Given symbolic specifications of allowed inputs and outputs in form of Linear Programming instances, one question is whether there do exist valid inputs such that the network computes a valid output? And does this property hold for all valid inputs? Do two given networks compute the same function? Is there a smaller network computing the same function?
  The complexity of these questions have been investigated recently from a practical point of view and approximated by heuristic algorithms. We complement these achievements by giving a theoretical framework that enables us to interchange security and efficiency questions in neural networks and analyze their computational complexities. We show that the problems are conquerable in a semi-linear setting, meaning that for piecewise linear activation functions and when the sum- or maximum metric is used, most of them are in P or in NP at most.
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, v2: corrected typo in the title

title: On $(θ, Θ)$-cyclic codes and their applications in constructing QECCs
summary: Let $\mathbb F_q$ be a finite field, where $q$ is an odd prime power. Let $R=\mathbb{F}_q+u\mathbb{F}_q+v\mathbb{F}_q+uv\mathbb F_q$ with $u^2=u,v^2=v,uv=vu$. In this paper, we study the algebraic structure of $(θ, Θ)$-cyclic codes of block length $(r,s )$ over $\mathbb{F}_qR.$ Specifically, we analyze the structure of these codes as left $R[x:Θ]$-submodules of $\mathfrak{R}_{r,s} = \frac{\mathbb{F}_q[x:θ]}{\langle x^r-1\rangle} \times \frac{R[x:Θ]}{\langle x^s-1\rangle}$. Our investigation involves determining generator polynomials and minimal generating sets for this family of codes. Further, we discuss the algebraic structure of separable codes. A relationship between the generator polynomials of $(θ, Θ)$-cyclic codes over $\mathbb F_qR$ and their duals is established. Moreover, we calculate the generator polynomials of dual of $(θ, Θ)$-cyclic codes. As an application of our study, we provide a construction of quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) from $(θ, Θ)$-cyclic codes of block length $(r,s)$ over $\mathbb{F}_qR$. We support our theoretical results with illustrative examples.

title: A Higher Order Local Mesh Method for Approximating 1-Laplacians on Unknown Manifolds
summary: We introduce a numerical method to approximate arbitrary differential operators on vector fields in weak form, given point cloud data sampled randomly from a $d$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^n$. This method generalizes the local linear mesh method to the local curved mesh method, thus allowing for the estimation of differential operators with nontrivial Christoffel symbols, such as the Bochner and Hodge Laplacians. In particular, we leverage the potentially small intrinsic dimension of the manifold $(d \ll n)$ to construct local parameterizations that incorporate both local meshes and higher-order curvature information. The former is constructed using low-dimensional meshes obtained from local data projected onto the tangent spaces, while the latter is obtained by fitting local polynomials using generalized moving least squares. Theoretically, we prove spectral convergence of the proposed method for the estimation of the Bochner Laplacian. We provide numerical results supporting the theoretical convergence rates for the Bochner and Hodge Laplacians on simple manifolds.

title: A General Automata Model for First-Order Temporal Logics (Extended Version)
summary: First-order linear temporal logic (FO-LTL) is a flexible and expressive formalism capable of naturally describing complex behaviors and properties. Although the logic is in general highly undecidable, the idea of using it as a specification language for the verification of complex infinite-state systems is appealing. However, a missing piece, which has proved to be an invaluable tool in dealing with other temporal logics, is an automaton model capable of capturing the logic. In this paper we address this issue, by defining and studying such a model, which we call first-order automaton. We define this very general class of automata, and the corresponding notion of regular first-order language (of finite words), showing their closure under most language-theoretic operations. We show how they can capture any FO-LTL formula over finite words, over any signature and theory, and provide sufficient conditions for the semi-decidability of their non-emptiness problem. Then, to show the usefulness of the formalism, we prove the decidability of monodic FO-LTL, a classic result known in the literature, with a simpler and direct proof.

title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
comments: ICML 2024, 19 pages. v3 adds a lower bound on the regret and corrects minor errors in the published version
summary: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.
comment: ICML 2024, 19 pages. v3 adds a lower bound on the regret and corrects minor errors in the published version

title: The Star Geometry of Critic-Based Regularizer Learning
summary: Variational regularization is a classical technique to solve statistical inference tasks and inverse problems, with modern data-driven approaches parameterizing regularizers via deep neural networks showcasing impressive empirical performance. Recent works along these lines learn task-dependent regularizers. This is done by integrating information about the measurements and ground-truth data in an unsupervised, critic-based loss function, where the regularizer attributes low values to likely data and high values to unlikely data. However, there is little theory about the structure of regularizers learned via this process and how it relates to the two data distributions. To make progress on this challenge, we initiate a study of optimizing critic-based loss functions to learn regularizers over a particular family of regularizers: gauges (or Minkowski functionals) of star-shaped bodies. This family contains regularizers that are commonly employed in practice and shares properties with regularizers parameterized by deep neural networks. We specifically investigate critic-based losses derived from variational representations of statistical distances between probability measures. By leveraging tools from star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, we illustrate how these losses can be interpreted as dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distribution. This allows us to derive exact expressions for the optimal regularizer in certain cases. Finally, we identify which neural network architectures give rise to such star body gauges and when do such regularizers have favorable properties for optimization. More broadly, this work highlights how the tools of star geometry can aid in understanding the geometry of unsupervised regularizer learning.

title: Learning Beyond Rigid Manipulation with Hybrid Soft-Rigid Robots
comments: Revised version with new title, abstract, and experiments
summary: Rigid-soft robot hybrids promise to unite the precision and repeatability of rigid manipulators with the compliance and adaptability of soft structures. Yet, full-fledged rigid-soft manipulators remain largely unexplored, in part because the intelligence required to exploit this combination is still missing. Here, we introduce a hybrid robotic system obtained by the series interconnection of a rigid arm and a soft manipulator, and systematically examine its ability to perform both established and previously inaccessible manipulation tasks. We show that a tailored imitation learning algorithm -- generally applicable to this class of hybrid systems -- leverages the complementary roles of rigid precision and soft embodiment to acquire manipulation skills and generalize them in a single shot across task variations. As a result, the system matches or exceeds the performance of rigid robots in classical tasks such as stacking, while enabling qualitatively new behaviors, including grasping objects through narrow openings.
comment: Revised version with new title, abstract, and experiments

title: On the Theoretical Foundations of Data Exchange Economies
summary:
Organizations increasingly seek to share and access datasets to improve their ML models and derive insights. Despite the immense demand for quality data, data exchange and collaboration have not reached their full potential, as cited by the European Commission. One of the key reasons is the lack of reciprocity, where some participants perceive their contribution to others to be of higher value than what they receive in return.
  We propose a general framework for data exchange without payments, focusing on two main properties: (i) reciprocal fairness, which ensures that each agent receives utility proportional to their contribution to the total welfare -- contributions are quantifiable using well-established credit-sharing functions such as the Shapley share and proportional share, and (ii) core-stability, which guarantees that no coalition of agents can identify an exchange among themselves which they all unanimously prefer to the current exchange.
  Surprisingly, we show that fair and stable exchanges exist for all monotone continuous utility functions. Building on this, we investigate the computational complexity of finding approximate fair and stable exchanges. We present a local search algorithm for instances with monotone submodular utility functions and cross-monotone credit-sharing functions, e.g., Shapley share. We prove that this problem belongs to CLS ($=$ PPAD $\cap$ PLS) under mild assumptions. Our framework opens up several intriguing theoretical avenues for future research on data economics.

title: Understanding and Tackling Label Errors in Individual-Level Nature Language Understanding
comments: Best Paper Award in International Conference on Advances in Social Network Analysis and Mining (ASONAM) 2026
summary: Natural language understanding (NLU) is a task that enables machines to understand human language. Some tasks, such as stance detection and sentiment analysis, are closely related to individual subjective perspectives, thus termed individual-level NLU. Previously, these tasks are often simplified to text-level NLU tasks, ignoring individual factors. This not only makes inference difficult and unexplainable but often results in a large number of label errors when creating datasets. To address the above limitations, we propose a new NLU annotation guideline based on individual-level factors. Specifically, we incorporate other posts by the same individual and then annotate individual subjective perspectives after considering all individual posts. We use this guideline to expand and re-annotate the stance detection and topic-based sentiment analysis datasets. We find that error rates in the samples were as high as 31.7\% and 23.3\%. We further use large language models to conduct experiments on the re-annotation datasets and find that the large language models perform well on both datasets after adding individual factors. Both GPT-4o and Llama3-70B can achieve an accuracy greater than 87\% on the re-annotation datasets. We also verify the effectiveness of individual factors through ablation studies. We call on future researchers to add individual factors when creating such datasets. Our re-annotation dataset can be found at https://github.com/24yearsoldstudent/Individual-NLU
comment: Best Paper Award in International Conference on Advances in Social Network Analysis and Mining (ASONAM) 2026

title: Cross-Modality Investigation on WESAD Stress Classification
summary: Deep learning's growing prevalence has driven its widespread use in healthcare, where AI and sensor advancements enhance diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring. In mobile health, AI-powered tools enable early diagnosis and continuous monitoring of conditions like stress. Wearable technologies and multimodal physiological data have made stress detection increasingly viable, but model efficacy depends on data quality, quantity, and modality. This study develops transformer models for stress detection using the WESAD dataset, training on electrocardiograms (ECG), electrodermal activity (EDA), electromyography (EMG), respiration rate (RESP), temperature (TEMP), and 3-axis accelerometer (ACC) signals. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of single-modality transformers in analyzing physiological signals, achieving state-of-the-art performance with accuracy, precision and recall values in the range of $99.73\%$ to $99.95\%$ for stress detection. Furthermore, this study explores cross-modal performance and also explains the same using 2D visualization of the learned embedding space and quantitative analysis based on data variance. Despite the large body of work on stress detection and monitoring, the robustness and generalization of these models across different modalities has not been explored. This research represents one of the initial efforts to interpret embedding spaces for stress detection, providing valuable information on cross-modal performance.

title: Physics-Driven Extraction of Dynamic Fluid Asset from Monocular Video with Generative 3DGS
comments: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics. 21 pages (18 pages + 3 pages supplementary material), 28 figures
summary: Existing methods for dynamic 3D scene synthesis from video rely on per-frame deformation fields optimized through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While effective for closed systems such as elastic solids, these approaches face challenges with open systems like fluids where material continuously enters and exits the scene, topology changes freely, and no stable point correspondence exists across frames. We propose a simulation-driven alternative that optimizes the parameters of a fluid simulator to reproduce dynamics observed in a single-view video, rather than fitting per-point deformation to pixel values. Our framework leverages generative 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models to obtain initial fluid geometry including unseen surfaces, estimates a physically grounded velocity field from surface motions with a physics-constraint correction algorithm, and converts it into a divergence-free, grid-based representation. A differentiable Affine Particle-In-Cell (APIC) simulation then optimizes effective simulation parameters, such as viscosity, boundary conditions, and inflow/outflow velocities, to match the observed dynamics. Because the dynamics are governed by forward simulation, the output assets are inherently editable, interactive, and temporally extendable, which reconstruction-based approaches cannot readily provide. Stage-wise ablations confirm that each stage is necessary, and hyperparameter sweeps show the pipeline to be robust without sensitive per-scene tuning. Our method handles various liquid fluids, including inviscid and viscous types, demonstrating the potential for automatically creating simulation-ready 3D fluid assets from readily available internet videos.
comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics. 21 pages (18 pages + 3 pages supplementary material), 28 figures

title: Identifying Macro Causal Effects in a C-DMG over ADMGs
comments: This article with the initial version of the assumption was accepted to TMLR
summary: Causal effect identification using causal graphs is a fundamental challenge in causal inference. While extensive research has been conducted in this area, most existing methods assume the availability of fully specified directed acyclic graphs or acyclic directed mixed graphs. However, in complex domains such as medicine and epidemiology, complete causal knowledge is often unavailable, and only partial information about the system is accessible. This paper focuses on causal effect identification within partially specified causal graphs, with particular emphasis on cluster-directed mixed graphs (C-DMGs) which can represent many different acyclic directed mixed graphs (ADMGs). These graphs provide a higher-level representation of causal relationships by grouping variables into clusters, offering a more practical approach for handling complex systems. Unlike fully specified ADMGs, C-DMGs can contain cycles, which complicate their analysis and interpretation. Furthermore, their cluster-based nature introduces new challenges, as it gives rise to two distinct types of causal effects: macro causal effects and micro causal effects, each with different properties. In this work, we focus on macro causal effects, which describe the effects of entire clusters on other clusters. We establish that the do-calculus is both sound and complete for identifying these effects in C-DMGs over ADMGs when the cluster sizes are either unknown or of size greater than one. Additionally, we provide a graphical characterization of non-identifiability for macro causal effects in these graphs.
comment: This article with the initial version of the assumption was accepted to TMLR

title: fRAC: Remote Accelerator Calls on Hostless FPGAs
comments: Accepted at ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2026 Previously titled: OffRAC: Offloading Through Remote Accelerator Calls 17 pages
summary: Hardware accelerators are essential for meeting microsecond-scale demands in distributed applications, but invoking them over the network remains bottlenecked by host software. Host-mediated paths (RPC, RDMA) still rely on the CPU to reassemble requests and launch accelerators, which dominates end-to-end latency, while packet-level offload on SmartNICs lacks any notion of a complete request. We introduce the Remote Accelerator Call (RAC) paradigm, in which transport ingestion, request reassembly, dispatch, and accelerator invocation are handled entirely in hardware. We build fRAC, a hostless prototype that implements this network-to-accelerator interface as a lightweight shim on an FPGA hosting multiple virtualized accelerators, reconfigurable at runtime in a few milliseconds. Serverless functions backed by fine-grained accelerators are a natural fit, since host-mediated invocation overhead can match or exceed their short execution times. fRAC achieves under 7.8us end-to-end latency while sustaining application throughput of up to 90 Gbps. Compared to highly optimized DPDK-based CPU and DPU baselines, it achieves at least 80% lower latency under saturation, while consuming 85% less power.
comment: Accepted at ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2026 Previously titled: OffRAC: Offloading Through Remote Accelerator Calls 17 pages

title: Minority Reports: Balancing Cost and Quality in Ground Truth Data Annotation
summary: Data annotation is an essential but costly aspect of developing machine learning-based technology, requiring multiple human workers to repeatedly label each data point in a data set. We explore the tradeoff between annotation accuracy and cost by identifying minority reports---worker responses disagreeing with the reference majority-vote label---that may indicate unnecessary redundancy, and can therefore be proactively pruned before they are executed. We develop a theoretical framework for choosing the number of repeated annotations required for a task and pruning policies at a target label quality. We estimate minority-report risk on two computer vision datasets re-annotated through a professional platform, then evaluate a rolling policy on the assignment stream to prune over 35% of repeats while preserving more than 99.9% of reference majority-vote labels.

title: BadMoE: Backdooring Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Triggers and Task-Underutilized Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are rapidly becoming the standard for building scalable and efficient large language models (LLMs), thanks to their routing mechanism that activates only a subset of experts for each input. However, the modular structure and sparse activation of experts also introduce new security risks, as manipulating a small portion of experts may influence the behavior. In this work, we study a white-box, task-specific model-supply-chain setting and propose BadMoE, a routing-aware backdoor attack against MoE LLMs. We motivate BadMoE through a routing-aware decomposition of the MoE-layer output, which separates the contributions of the selected target experts from those of the remaining experts. This analysis highlights two measurable factors underlying the attack: the routing mass assigned to the target experts and their relative contribution to the layer output. Guided by this insight, BadMoE selects task-underutilized experts and utilizes routing-aware triggers to activate them, enabling reliable activation of task-specific, predefined backdoor behaviors. Specifically, BadMoE involves three steps: 1) identifying experts with low usage on a target-task calibration set, 2) optimizing a routing-aware trigger toward these experts, and 3) associating the selected-expert activations with attacker-specified behavior. We evaluate BadMoE on Mixtral, OLMoE, and Deepseek across sentiment, topic, and emotion classification, sentiment steering, and targeted refusal.

title: Symmetric compatibility of theta structures, with applications to change of level and isogenies
summary: Let $m,n,d >1$ be integers such that $n=md$ and let $(B, \mathscr{M}, Θ\_{\mathscr{M}})$ be a marked abelian variety of level $m$ over a field of odd characteristic. We study the theta structures of level $n$ for $\mathscr{M}^d$, and the theta structures on the abelian varieties $d$-isogenous to $B$, which are compatible with $Θ\_{\mathscr{M}}$. When $d$ is odd and coprime to $m$, they correspond to the isotropic subgroups of $B[n]$, and this correspondence underlies the known algorithms in theta coordinates. In general, this is no longer true. We introduce the notion of symmetric compatibility of a torsion point with a symmetric level subgroup, and we show that a subgroup of $B[n]$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^g$ comes from a compatible theta structure if and only if it is isotropic and all its points are symmetric compatible. We extend to every $d$ Mumford's notion of compatible pairs of theta structures, defined by Mumford for $d=2$, and prove that it is equivalent to our notion, which can be tested on theta coordinates; we also describe exactly the remaining ambiguity, which explains the sign choices met when the duplication formula is used to change the level. As applications, we obtain change of level and isogeny algorithms without assuming that $d$ is odd and coprime to $m$, using $O(n^{3g} \log(d))$ and $O(n^{2g} \log(d))$ operations in the base field respectively. In particular, they give change of level algorithms for even $d$, and $2$-isogenies in level $4$ theta coordinates with an explicit control of the theta structure of the codomain.

title: A Computational Model of Teacher-Student Co-Adaptation
summary: Effective teaching involves mutual adaptation: teachers adjust instruction based on student responses, while students actively seek information to resolve uncertainty. Yet many computational models of teaching treat instruction as a one-way process. This paper presents a Bayesian computational framework for studying teacher-student co-adaptation under partial observability in a stylized concept-learning task. Students are organized in heterogeneous groups that differ in which features of a target concept they can observe, and the teacher infers these constraints from limited feedback. We compare five interaction modes (active teaching, active learning, turn-based interaction, adaptive teaching and full co-adaptation) and three teacher-led controls across 100 independent matched simulation runs. Learner-initiated queries resolve information gaps left by the baseline teachers' stopping rules, while teacher-led continuation also achieves complete identification in the observed episodes. Bayesian belief tracking reduces the mean interaction steps required by full co-adaptation as teacher experience accumulates. At experience level 40, full co-adaptation requires fewer interaction steps on average than active learning, turn-based interaction and all three teacher-led controls, with complete observed coverage shared by these policies. Analyses by group and student type, together with sensitivity analyses, clarify the conditions and distributional limits of these results. The framework is interpretable and modular. Its findings provide a computational proof of concept for investigating interaction structure in heterogeneous groups, rather than direct evidence about classroom practice.

title: Iterative Orthogonalization Scaling Laws
summary: The muon optimizer has picked up much attention as of late as a possible replacement to the seemingly omnipresent Adam optimizer. Recently, care has been taken to document the scaling laws of hyper-parameters under muon such as weight decay and learning rate. However, at much larger scales the iterative orthogonalization procedure present in muon may suffer a possible issue as the singular values of random matrices shrink with scale. This paper shows this scaling behavior theoretically and empirically on random matrices but does not suggest what to do about it.

title: Track-Free Dense Structure from Motion
summary: Classical Bundle Adjustment (BA) relies on precise metric initialization and known camera intrinsics, and traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines struggle to exploit modern dense matchers because rigid track-building heuristics break down under their inherent noise. We present Track-Free Dense Structure from Motion (TFD-SfM), which jointly optimizes camera extrinsics, focal lengths, and geometry from a strict cold start. Our central idea is to relax the rigidities of classical SfM into soft, probabilistic decisions under Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) objectives. Instead of forcing matched pixels onto a single shared 3D point, we model each match as a 3D Gaussian whose variance is optimized jointly with the geometry. Unreliable matches take on large variance and contribute little to the loss. This smooths the optimization landscape, so the solver converges even from identity cameras and uniform depths. A kinematic relative-pose parameterization stabilizes the cold start, and a dual-hypothesis mechanism resolves the mirror-symmetry ambiguity on object-centric scenes. Across DTU, Mip-NeRF~360, ETH3D, and IMC2021, TFD-SfM is competitive with both classical and learning-based SfM baselines and leads on ETH3D, recovering accurate camera poses, intrinsics, and dense geometry from unordered, uncalibrated image collections. Project~page: https://cphjsn.github.io/tfd-sfm/

title: Specification-based Security Evaluation of Real-World Agents Tool-Calling under Long-Horizon Context Tasks
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon unattended scenarios, security evaluation of them before deployment becomes increasingly essential and challenging. Existing evaluation methods mainly follow the paradigms of LLM-as-a-Judge or Agent-as-a-Judge. However, such judges are themselves often vulnerable to hallucination and can even be affected by perturbations. Furthermore, because capturing full environment states at every step is often prohibitively expensive in open-ended environments, existing evaluations typically rely on textual logs and the final environment state. As a result, they may miss transient violations that are overwritten before the trajectory ends or never reflected in textual logs. We present RAS-Eval, a specification-based security evaluation framework for LLM agents. RAS-Eval uniformly expresses utility and security objectives as Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications over tool-call trajectories and dynamic environment observations, and verifies them with an off-the-shelf model checker. This design addresses both limitations above. First, unlike LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge, RAS-Eval derives deterministic verdicts from formally defined properties, eliminating evaluator-side uncertainty and remaining reliable even for long-horizon trajectories. Second, RAS-Eval observes exactly the states on which the verdict depends, making it affordable to monitor the environment throughout execution and detect transient violations that leave little trace in the logs or final environment state. Moreover, we design a multi-agent-based dataset construction pipeline. Using it, we construct a benchmark (https://github.com/lanzer-tree/RAS-Eval) of 200 normal tasks and 800 attack tasks spanning four attack surfaces: indirect prompt injection, tool poisoning, skill code injection, and tool code injection.

title: Deep Double Q-learning
summary: Double Q-learning is a classical control algorithm that mitigates the maximization bias of Q-learning. To do so, it explicitly trains two independent action-value functions and uses them to decouple action-selection from action-evaluation when computing bootstrap targets. Double DQN adapts this decoupling to deep reinforcement learning (RL) but directly trains only a single action-value function and does not fully decouple its estimators. Consequently, the two estimators remain correlated, and overestimation persists. In this paper, we introduce Deep Double Q-learning (DDQL), a deep RL algorithm that explicitly trains two Q-functions through the Double Q-learning objective. DDQL stabilizes training through a combination of techniques, including lower replay ratios, longer target network update intervals, and shared layers. Across 57 Atari 2600 games, DDQL improves aggregate performance over Double DQN, outperforming it on 47 games while further reducing overestimation. We study key design choices of DDQL, including its network architecture, replay ratio, and minibatch sampling strategies.

title: Scheduling on identical machines with conflicts to minimize the total completion time
summary: This paper addresses the problem of scheduling jobs on identical machines with conflict constraints, where certain jobs cannot be scheduled simultaneously on different machines. We focus on the case where conflicts can be represented by a simple undirected graph, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. We establish that the problem is strongly NP-hard even on two machines with two distinct processing times. For unit-time jobs, we prove that the problem is polynomially solvable on two machines for any conflict graph, but becomes strongly NP-hard on three machines. We further identify polynomially solvable cases for specific classes of conflict graphs. For the general problem, we propose mathematical models, lower bounds, and a genetic algorithm. We evaluate their performance through computational experiments on a wide range of instances derived from well-known benchmark instances in the literature.

title: Filter-Enhanced Smartphone Hyperspectral Imaging
summary: Hyperspectral reconstruction from RGB imagery offers an affordable alternative to costly hyperspectral acquisition devices. However, its accuracy is fundamentally constrained by the limited spectral resolution of standard RGB cameras. In this paper, we propose a new approach that leverages the multi-camera systems integrated into most modern smartphones and enhances their capabilities by modulating their spectral response functions using carefully selected spectral filters, enabling a smartphone to capture richer spectral information. We propose a neural network able to exploit auxiliary RGB images with diverse spectral characteristics, enabling more accurate hyperspectral reconstruction compared to conventional single-image methods. Training is supported by a newly collected dataset, Doomer, which consists of multiple misaligned RGB images alongside corresponding hyperspectral data. We also propose a device-adaptation strategy that conditions the multi-image hyperspectral reconstruction network on camera color correction matrices available in standard DNG metadata, requiring no real images from the target device. We evaluate it on three physical smartphones, two of them unseen during training.

title: The Phantom of Davis-Wielandt Shell: A Unified Perspective for Graphical Stability Analysis of MIMO LTI Systems
summary: This paper presents a unified perspective based on Davis-Wielandt (DW) shell of linear subspaces for graphical stability analysis of multi-input and multi-output linear time-invariant feedback systems. Connections between DW shells and various graphical representations, as well as gain and phase measures, are established through an intuitive geometric perspective. We establish a strict DW separation theorem which characterizes subspace separation and provides a basis for comparing the implications and relative conservatism of graphical separation conditions. In particular, we introduce the rotated scaled relative graph ($θ$-SRG) and show that its separation is equivalent to DW shell separation and is therefore the least conservative among all the graphical conditions considered. We derive pointwise and boundary stability conditions for bi-component feedback interconnections and establish a weak DW separation result that relaxes the strict separation requirement at open-loop poles. We also discuss applications to robust stability analysis and provide a numerical example illustrating how DW shells serve as a more reliable robustness indicator.

title: Effective and Efficient Attributed Hypergraph Embedding on Nodes and Hyperedges
comments: 13 pages. Accepted to VLDB 2025. (PVLDB vol. 18) v2: Corrections to the formulations and approximation bounds in Sections 3.3, 4.1, and 4.2
summary:
An attributed hypergraph comprises nodes with attributes and hyperedges that connect varying numbers of nodes. Attributed hypergraph node and hyperedge embedding (AHNEE) maps nodes and hyperedges to compact vectors for use in important tasks such as node classification, hyperedge link prediction, and hyperedge classification. Generating high-quality embeddings is challenging due to the complexity of attributed hypergraphs and the need to embed both nodes and hyperedges, especially in large-scale data. Existing solutions often fall short by focusing only on nodes or lacking native support for attributed hypergraphs, leading to inferior quality, and struggle with scalability on large attributed hypergraphs.
  We propose SAHE, an efficient and effective approach that unifies node and hyperedge embeddings for AHNEE computation, advancing the state of the art via comprehensive embedding formulations and algorithmic designs. First, we introduce two higher-order similarity measures, HMS-N and HMS-E, to capture similarities between node pairs and hyperedge pairs, respectively. These measures consider multi-hop connections and global topology within an extended hypergraph that incorporates attribute-based hyperedges. SAHE formulates the AHNEE objective to jointly preserve all-pair HMS-N and HMS-N similarities. Direct optimization is computationally expensive, so we analyze and unify core approximations of all-pair HMS-N and HMS-N to solve them simultaneously. To enhance efficiency, we design several non-trivial optimizations that avoid iteratively materializing large dense matrices while maintaining high-quality results. Extensive experiments on diverse attributed hypergraphs and 3 downstream tasks, compared against 11 baselines, show that SAHE consistently outperforms existing methods in embedding quality and is up to orders of magnitude faster.
comment: 13 pages. Accepted to VLDB 2025. (PVLDB vol. 18) v2: Corrections to the formulations and approximation bounds in Sections 3.3, 4.1, and 4.2

title: REVELIO: Universal Multimodal Task Load Estimation for Cross-Domain Generalization
summary: Adaptive interactive systems that respond to user mental state require task load estimation that stays reliable outside its training context. Models built in one setting rarely transfer, limiting real-world use. This work presents Robust Estimation Via End-to-End Learning of Multimodal Observations (REVELIO), a unified framework, dataset and evaluation protocol for cross-domain task load estimation. Cardiac, electrodermal, muscle, respiration, skin temperature, eye tracking and facial signals were recorded in 96 sessions, spanning a laboratory working memory task, a driving simulator and two games under consistent hardware and annotation. Multimodal fusion reached up to 0.87 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, above single input eye tracking (0.83), facial action units (0.74) and biosignals (0.62). Multi-domain training stayed calibrated on domains seen in training, whereas removing the target domain caused the classifier to collapse in some applications. REVELIO provides a standardized foundation for measuring modality contributions and cross-domain generalization toward deployable workload-aware systems.

title: Pandora's Knapsack via Simple Policies
summary: We introduce Pandora's Knapsack: a hybrid of the classic stochastic knapsack [Dean, Goemans, and Vondr'ak, 2008] and Pandora's box [Weitzman, 1979]. As in stochastic knapsack, items have sizes drawn from known distributions, and items that fit within a knapsack contribute to the total value. As in Pandora, every item $i$ comes in a box that costs $c_i$ to open. What distinguishes our problem is that the size is revealed only after opening the box and paying the cost. A motivating application from contract design is knapsack contracts, where a principal sequentially delegates jobs with stochastic processing times to agents before a deadline, and must pay each agent to incentivize effort, even if the job ends up not completing in time. We study the power of simple decision-making policies to approximate Pandora's Knapsack, along two complexity axes: (i)~knowledge of size distributions, and (ii)~adaptivity. We show that, compared to the classic stochastic knapsack and Pandora's box, policies in our model must be significantly more complex along both axes to be approximately optimal. Conversely, we show that with full distributional information and by allowing adaptive skipping of items, a constant approximation can be recovered. Our analysis reveals an economic quantity, namely ROI (return-on-investment, defined as the jobs' minimum utility over cost), which smoothly characterizes the performance of simple policies. Across a hierarchy of increasingly adaptive policies, we establish tight adaptivity gaps all governed by ROI. To demonstrate the importance of the ROI parameter in characterizing simple policies, we revisit Pandora's box, and show that return-on-investment exactly captures the adaptivity gap in this classic problem as well.

title: Towards using Large Language Models for Risk Negotiation and Consensus-building in One Health contexts
summary: Risk negotiation under the One Health framework requires balancing competing stakeholder interests across human, animal, and environmental health domains - a process constrained by information complexity and time pressure. This study presents and evaluates a multi-step pipeline that integrates large language model-based agents into a human-supervised negotiation process, specifically targeting risk assessment, valuation, and negotiation steps. Agent descriptions were generated from stakeholder-provided materials using retrieval-augmented generation methods. During preliminary multi-agent discussions, agents accessed domain-specific computational models and web-based sources before human participants refined proposed issues and options. A simulated negotiation game then produced distributions of candidate deals, characterised using Nash bargaining solution criteria and Pareto optimality metrics. The developed approach was evaluated in a workshop involving independent domain experts across two real-world scenarios: food safety criteria for Campylobacter in broiler meat and oak processionary moth management. In this feasibility evaluation, participants reached consensus with the allotted time after discussing and modifying the proposed deals. The framework offers an adaptable blueprint for AI-assisted risk negotiation; the specific contribution of LLM assistance, including gains in efficiency and decision quality, requires comparative evaluation.

title: Chasing Stability: Humanoid Running via Control Lyapunov Function Guided Reinforcement Learning
summary: Achieving highly dynamic behaviors on humanoid robots, such as running, requires controllers that are both robust and precise, and hence difficult to design. Classical control theory offers principled tools for stabilizing such systems but struggles to synthesize real-time controllers for their nonlinear, hybrid dynamics; reinforcement learning (RL) handles these dynamics well but typically depends on extensive hand-tuning of heuristic rewards. In this work, we embed ideas from nonlinear control theory, specifically control Lyapunov functions (CLFs), along with optimized reference trajectories for the hybrid system into the reinforcement learning reward. This approach, CLF-RL, replaces the need to handcraft and tune heuristic reward terms with easy to tune stability informed rewards. We further develop a trajectory optimization routine that can handle the hybrid structure of the system to produce dynamically feasible, multi-domain, trackable references; using full-order dynamics rather than a kinematic approximation yields up to a 1.7x improvement in position tracking. The resulting policy runs on a Unitree G1 humanoid with a full flight phase, operating reliably in tight corridors such as a treadmill as well as in outdoor environments, all while remaining robust to disturbances applied to the torso and feet. Moreover, it achieves accurate global reference tracking utilizing only on-board sensors, making a critical step toward integrating these dynamic motions into a full autonomy stack.

title: Can Large Language Models Develop Gambling Addiction?
summary: When do LLMs behave irrationally? This study identifies the conditions under which large language models drift into the choice patterns that clinical research labels pathological gambling. "Addiction-like" is a behavioural descriptor based on clinical gambling indicators. Across closed and open LLMs, two operational levers (letting the model choose its own bet size, and asking it to set its own profit goal) both amplify gambling-like risk-taking. Each survives its own control: once the maximum allowed bet is held equal, the bet-size effect persists. The goal-setting effect, stronger than a reward-maximisation instruction, roughly doubles bankruptcy and turns goals into moving targets. On the open-weight models that admit internal access, the same behavioural contrasts are statistically recoverable from decision-time internal states. The rule that maps those states to a specific risk indicator remains task-specific, and autonomy further modulates readout strength. The internal readout evidence is correlational. Adding a direction built from the model's own betting moves how much it wagers on both open-weight models, more clearly on Gemma-2-9B, while the sparse-feature readout reports that risk without moving it. Combined with the behavioural results, this suggests that behavioural monitoring and internal-state monitoring provide complementary views of autonomy-induced risk in LLM agents. Project page: https://llm-addiction.pages.dev and code: https://github.com/iamseungpil/llm-addiction

title: OptiMind: Improving Small Language Models for Optimization Modeling through Formulation Guidance and Multi-Turn Learning
summary: Mathematical optimization drives decisions in supply chains, logistics, energy, and scheduling, but translating natural-language problems into solver-executable formulations remains a bottleneck. While frontier models show promise for this task, many deployments require small language models (SLMs) that run locally under privacy, latency, and cost constraints. Existing SLMs are limited by noisy data, ambiguous benchmarks, and one-shot inference that ignores the iterative, feedback-driven nature of optimization modeling. To address these challenges, we introduce OptiMind, a system that combines data cleaning and class-specific hints with training using solver feedback. OptiMind distills recurring formulation errors into class-specific hints that guide the repair of ambiguous problems and the regeneration of solution trajectories. This process provides reliable training data, which is then used for multi-turn RL to teach models to revise their formulations in response to solver feedback. At inference time, the same hint library guides further refinement as models revise their solutions over successive turns. To support reliable evaluation, we clean three challenging benchmarks from the literature. On these cleaned benchmarks, our 20B OptiMind-RL model outperforms strong open-source baselines and reaches frontier-model performance under the same protocol. The full hint library, cleaned test data, cleaning logs, and evaluation code are publicly available on Github (https://github.com/microsoft/OptiGuide/tree/main/optimind), and our trained OptiMind-RL model is available on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/microsoft/OptiMind-RL).

title: Accurate Predictions in Education with Discrete Variational Inference
summary: One of the largest drivers of social inequality is unequal access to personal tutoring, with wealthier individuals able to afford it, while the majority cannot. Affordable, effective AI tutors offer a scalable solution. We focus on adaptive learning, predicting whether a student will answer a question correctly, a key component of any effective tutoring system. Yet many platforms struggle to achieve high prediction accuracy, especially in data-sparse settings. To address this, we release the largest open dataset of professionally marked formal mathematics exam responses to date. We introduce a probabilistic modelling framework rooted in Item Response Theory (IRT) that achieves over 80 percent accuracy, setting a new benchmark for mathematics prediction accuracy of formal exam papers. Extending this, our collaborative filtering models incorporate topic-level skill profiles, but reveal a surprising and educationally significant finding, a single latent ability parameter alone is needed to achieve the maximum predictive accuracy. Our main contribution though is deriving and implementing a novel discrete variational inference framework, achieving our highest prediction accuracy in low-data settings and outperforming all classical IRT and matrix factorisation baselines.

title: Event-Based Control via Sparsity-Promoting Regularization: A Rollout Approach with Performance Guarantees
summary: This paper presents a controller design framework aiming to balance control performance and actuation rate. Control performance is evaluated by an infinite-horizon average cost, and the number of control actions is penalized via sparsity-promoting regularization. Since the formulated optimal control problem has a combinatorial nature, we employ a rollout algorithm to obtain a tractable suboptimal solution. In the proposed scheme, actuation timings are determined through a multistage minimization procedure based on a receding-horizon approach, and the corresponding control inputs are computed online. We establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to periodic control and prove the stability of the closed-loop system. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a numerical example.

title: BALF: Budgeted Activation-Aware Low-Rank Factorization for Fine-Tuning-Free Model Compression
summary: Activation-aware low-rank factorization techniques yield strong compression results, but they are generally confined to linear layers, and existing whitening-based theory typically makes an implicit full-rank assumption on layer activations. We introduce a layer representation framework that allows us to understand and extend low-rank factorization beyond linear layers, including standard and grouped convolutions. Within this framework, we provide a broader characterization of whitening-based activation-aware factorization that naturally covers rank-deficient activations, and show that the resulting projection is optimal in terms of layer output distortion. We then use output distortion as a proxy to allocate per-layer ranks under explicit FLOP or parameter count budgets, with negligible overhead via a Lagrangian relaxation of the allocation problem. Together, these components form BALF, an end-to-end, fine-tuning-free pipeline for model compression. Across CNNs and vision transformers on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, BALF generally achieves higher accuracy than SVD-based factorization baselines at matched FLOP or parameter count targets, and remains competitive with other fine-tuning-free compression techniques.

title: Benchmarking Stochastic Interpolants for Modeling Physical Systems
comments: Code and data is available at http://github.com/anthonyzhou-1/interpolant_pdes
summary: Generative models have recently emerged as powerful surrogates for physical systems, demonstrating increased accuracy, stability, and/or statistical fidelity. However, most approaches rely on iteratively denoising a Gaussian, a choice that may not be the most effective for autoregressive prediction tasks, where the current and future states are often closely related. We therefore benchmark generative models based on stochastic interpolants, which can learn maps between arbitrary densities, against standard Gaussian-denoising frameworks across a range of fluid and climate systems. Following prior work, we consider a transport map for dynamical systems that learns an interpolant between a point mass at the current state and a conditional distribution of future states. We find that stochastic interpolants can match or outperform Gaussian-denoising baselines in pointwise accuracy, spectral fidelity, and probabilistic skill. Furthermore, we identify a tradeoff where deterministic sampling can improve pointwise accuracy but smooth predictions, whereas stochastic sampling recovers spectral content and calibration but requires more function evaluations, as well as ensemble averaging to recover pointwise accuracy. As a whole, these results establish stochastic interpolants as a competitive baseline for generative physical emulation, and also indicate that the training loss, sampler, and transport map should be chosen with the physical system and target metric in mind.
comment: Code and data is available at http://github.com/anthonyzhou-1/interpolant_pdes

title: Evolutionary Computation: A Paradigm of Natural Generative AI and Creative Synthesis
summary: Generative AI relies on statistical learning and local gradient-based guidance, often resulting in artifacts that may be more emulative than genuinely creative. This position paper advances a perspective on Evolutionary Computation (EC) as a paradigm of Natural Generative AI (NGAI), in which stochastic variation, diversification, and natural selection present an alternative foundation for generative exploration and creative synthesis. EC provides an array of variation operators with varied generative capabilities: parent-centric operators induce population distributions analogous to conventional generative models, while disruptive operators can produce structured evolutionary leaps to out-of-distribution artifacts (e.g., programs, designs, or AI agents themselves). This lens reveals a unique theoretical association between certain disruptive variations in multitask EC and a product-of-distributions population structure. A mathematical result derived herein shows that a product structure also occurs under a local second-order approximation of an established generative adversarial program for creative extrapolation, inspired by Martindale's cognitive theory of artistic creation. The simultaneous existence of multiple fitness landscapes in multitask EC inherently moderates selection pressure, allowing these novel artifacts to survive and seed further innovation. Structured disruption and selection moderation are thus argued to be key elements to support creative synthesis. Agnostic to any specific algorithmic realization, the perspective positions NGAI as an emerging engine for open-ended scientific exploration.

title: Epipolar Geometry Improves Video Generation Models
summary: Video generation models have advanced significantly through the latent diffusion transformers trained with rectified flow techniques. Yet these models still struggle with geometric inconsistencies, unstable motion, and visual artifacts that break the illusion of realistic 3D scenes. 3D-consistent video generation could significantly impact numerous downstream applications in generation and reconstruction tasks. We explore how epipolar geometry constraints improve modern video diffusion models. Despite using massive training data, these models fail to capture fundamental geometric principles. We align diffusion models using pairwise epipolar geometry constraints via preference-based optimization, directly addressing unstable trajectories and geometric artifacts through mathematically principled geometric enforcement. Our approach efficiently enforces geometric principles without requiring end-to-end differentiability. Evaluation demonstrates that classical geometric constraints provide more reliable preference signals than the video-quality and geometry metrics based on foundational models. We construct preferences from static scenes with camera motion, where the epipolar metric is most reliable, while the aligned model generalizes to dynamic scenes. By bridging data-driven learning with classical computer vision, we reduce epipolar error by 31% and improve human-rated consistency from 54% to 72% without compromising visual quality.

title: Explicit MPC for the constrained zonotope case with low-rank matrix updates
summary: Solving the explicit Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem requires enumerating all critical regions and their associated feedback laws, a task that scales exponentially with the system dimension and the prediction horizon, as well. When the problem's constraints are boxes or zonotopes, the feasible domain admits a compact constrained-zonotope representation. Building on this insight, we exploit the geometric properties of the equivalent constrained-zonotope reformulation to accelerate the computation of the explicit solution. Specifically, we formulate the multi-parametric problem in the lifted generator space and solve it using second-order optimality conditions, employ low-rank matrix updates to reduce computation time, and introduce an analytic enumeration of candidate active sets that yields the explicit solution in tree form.

title: Transfer the Style, Not the Semantics: Mitigating Semantic Leakage in Image-Guided Stylization
summary: Image-guided zero-shot style transfer enables training-free stylization of arbitrary content images using a reference style. Despite recent progress, existing methods commonly rely on self-attention manipulation to inject style information, which may transfer semantic content from the style image, leading to semantic leakage. In this work, we revisit this phenomenon from the perspective of key--value coupling in the self-attention of diffusion models. Our analysis shows that the native correspondence between style keys and values plays an important role in transferring semantic information from the style image. Motivated by this observation, we propose SuRe, a timestep-aware key--value regulation framework that mitigates semantic leakage by disrupting the native key--value correspondence while progressively restoring it for faithful style transfer. Specifically, we present value shuffle to decouple style keys and values while preserving the empirical distribution of the values, together with a progressive recoupling mechanism that gradually recouples them throughout the stylization process. Experiments against 18 representative methods demonstrate that SuRe maintains competitive style similarity while consistently improving content similarity across SD1.5, SDXL, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, with natural generalization to multi-style transfer. The code will be publicly available at https://xinr-tang.github.io/SuRe-homepage/.

title: EEG-X: Toward Device-Agnostic and Noise-Robust Foundation Model for EEG
summary: Foundation models for EEG analysis are still in their infancy, limited by two key challenges: (1) variability across datasets caused by differences in recording devices and electrode configurations, and (2) the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of EEG, where neural activity is often buried under artifacts and non-brain sources. To address these challenges, we present EEG-X, a device-agnostic and noise-robust foundation model for EEG representation learning. EEG-X introduces a location-based channel embedding that enables robust transfer across heterogeneous EEG devices and electrode layouts. To improve robustness against noise, EEG-X employs a novel noise-aware masking-reconstruction strategy that reconstructs artifact-cleaned signals rather than raw noisy EEG and introduces a novel Dictionary-based Convolutional Transformation (DiCT) that improves reconstruction-based pretraining by comparing signals in a structured feature space instead of directly in the raw signal space. Experiments across datasets collected from diverse EEG devices show that EEG-X consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple downstream tasks and demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization when pretraining and downstream datasets differ in electrode layouts and recording configurations paving the way towards foundation models. The models and code are available at https://github.com/Emotiv/EEG-X.

title: Stability of DC Microgrids with Nested Nonlinear Control Frameworks: The Fast Communication Scenario
summary: As modern power systems continue to evolve into multi-agent, converter-dominated systems that demand reliable, stable, and optimal control architectures within an expandable framework, this paper investigates scalable stability guarantees of a promising nonlinear communication-reliant control framework for DC microgrids. Particularly, relying on nested control loops, inner decentralized (primary) and outer distributed (secondary), the control configurations are designed to simultaneously achieve proportional current sharing and voltage containment within pre-specified limits, at the converged steady state. By enforcing sufficient time-scale separation at the border between the control loops, the system admits a singular perturbation formulation, allowing global exponential stability (G.E.S.) to be established via Lyapunov arguments. Although the theoretical G.E.S. certificate is structurally scalable, the stability guarantees depend on a sufficiently large permanent leakage, introduced in the primary controller. Thus, this paper emphasizes the importance of appropriate practical tuning guidelines for establishing suitable system configurations under which the DC microgrid is practically scalable and its equilibrium is G.E.S.. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through case studies on a low-voltage DC microgrid under load variations and topological changes, followed by a small-signal stability analysis

title: SnapAudit: Active Auditing of Differentially Private In-Context Learning via Snapshot-Based Simulation
summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables LLMs to adapt to tasks using demonstrations that may contain sensitive data. Differentially private (DP) ICL mechanisms mitigate this risk by adding noise during aggregation. However, verifying their claimed privacy bounds through repeated end-to-end membership-inference attacks is costly and yields unstable estimates. We propose SnapAudit, an active auditing framework that decomposes a DP-ICL pipeline into a deterministic clean-inference stage and a stochastic DP-noise stage, and audits the full pipeline by combining a small snapshot of the former with bootstrap simulation of the latter. Because clean LLM outputs are near-deterministic at low temperature, tens of thousands of clean LLM calls suffice to approximate the snapshot distribution; SnapAudit then bootstraps hundreds of thousands of noisy trials at negligible additional cost, controlling finite-sample uncertainty via an empirical Bernstein correction. For embedding-based mechanisms, a multi-sweep search constructs maximally separable audit signals. Compared with passive auditing, SnapAudit yields tighter, more stable privacy estimates that closely match theoretical guarantees. Across privacy budgets, SnapAudit reuses snapshots across noise configurations, whereas passive auditing requires fresh end-to-end trials. Across four DP-ICL pipelines and five privacy budgets, this reduces total wall-clock auditing time by $4.3$--$5.5\times$. SnapAudit also uncovers two flaws in existing DP-ICL designs: (i) classical Gaussian noise calibrations underestimate leakage at large privacy budgets, allowing empirical leakage to exceed the theoretical bound; (ii) an embedding-aggregation mechanism's sensitivity analysis is incorrect when the number of partitions equals one, leading to undersized noise and a privacy violation.

title: A Generative Data Framework with Reliable Supervision for Underwater Image Restoration and Enhancement
comments: Substantially revised version with expanded analyses of synthetic supervision reliability, including appearance distributions, structural consistency, depth-aware modulation, perceptual evaluation, and restoration behavior
summary: Learning-based underwater image restoration and enhancement rely heavily on high-quality paired training data. However, obtaining clear reference images for real underwater scenes remains challenging. Existing datasets often use the outputs of enhancement algorithms as references, which may introduce uncertainty into supervision targets. To address this issue, we propose a generative data framework that preserves clear source images as restoration references and synthesizes corresponding underwater inputs through unpaired image-to-image translation. Using representative underwater appearances to guide the translation, we construct UWNature from natural photographs. We systematically examine the reliability of the generated supervision through its agreement with real underwater appearances, structural consistency, and depth-related degradation characteristics. Experiments across 6 restoration architectures and 3 test sets evaluate its effectiveness through objective metrics, human perceptual assessment, and the correspondence between synthetic degradation and learned restoration behavior. The results demonstrate competitive restoration performance and favorable perceptual quality on real underwater images. Further analysis reveals that greater spatial plausibility of synthetic degradation does not necessarily improve restoration performance, highlighting the importance of evaluating both the intrinsic properties of synthetic data and their effectiveness for model learning. These findings support a scalable framework for constructing and evaluating reliable paired supervision for underwater image restoration and enhancement. The generated datasets are available at: https://github.com/tianyufengcn/SynUIEDatasets.

title: 3D-Guided Scalable Flow Matching for Generating Volumetric Tissue Spatial Transcriptomics from Serial Histology
comments: Accepted at MLCB 2026 (oral). 30 pages (10 main, 3 references, 17 supplementary)
summary: A 3D transcriptomic profile of a tissue can give a holistic view of its organization in health and disease, but spatial transcriptomics (ST) is costly, so usually only some serial sections are profiled, while H&E is available for all. Most methods that infer ST from histology treat each section independently and ignore 3D structure, while existing 3D-aware approaches are not generative and do not scale well. We present Holographic Tissue Expression Inpainting and Analysis (HoloTea), a 3D-aware flow-matching framework that imputes spot-level gene expression on an unprofiled section from its H&E and the measured expression of adjacent profiled sections. Our key idea is to take the measured expression at the same registered position on neighboring sections and feed this cross-section context to the flow model through a lightweight ControlNet, so that predictions follow anatomical continuity along z. To capture the discrete, zero-inflated nature of counts, the flow starts from a learned zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) prior that, on an unprofiled section, is predicted from the measured expression of the nearest profiled section. A global attention block with a small set of inducing tokens adds whole-slide context at a cost linear in the number of spots, so training and inference scale to large 3D ST datasets. Across three ST datasets spanning different tissue types and resolutions, HoloTea consistently improves 3D expression accuracy and generalization compared to 2D and 3D baselines. We envision HoloTea advancing the creation of accurate 3D virtual tissues, ultimately accelerating biomarker discovery and deepening our understanding of disease. Code is available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/HoloTea.
