Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 μm to 80 μm commonly assumed in the literature.

title: Global Trends and Heterogeneity in Modified Adjusted Net Savings
summary: Modified adjusted net savings is a derived weak sustainability indicator obtained by subtracting education expenditure from adjusted net savings (ANS). Because ANS equals net national savings plus education expenditure minus natural-resource depletion and carbon dioxide damage, MANS isolates the savings and depletion components and is useful when education expenditure would otherwise dominate cross-country comparisons. This study documents the global distribution, long-run trends, and cross-country heterogeneity of MANS excluding particulate emission damage over 1990-2021. The accounting base is the World Bank World Development Indicators series NY.ADJ.SVNX.CD, and MANS is constructed by subtracting education expenditure from this series. We combine global maps, aggregate time series, country-level heatmaps, distributional statistics, and income group comparisons. The results show that global MANS has increased substantially in aggregate, but its evolution as a share of nominal GDP has been more volatile and uneven across countries. Per capita MANS and global MANS totals remain concentrated in high-income and large economies, whereas low-income and lower-middle-income groups display persistently lower and more volatile outcomes. Country rankings are highly persistent, and some populous countries exhibit pronounced fluctuations associated with natural-resource dependence and structural change. The study provides a reproducible descriptive benchmark for monitoring sustainable development and highlights the need to interpret MANS in current US dollars alongside income-group and country-specific contexts. The findings are relevant for macroeconomic policy, natural-capital accounting, and the design of sustainability-oriented investment strategies.

title: Causal Learning with Invalid Instruments for High-dimensional Imaging Responses
summary: Large-scale neuroimaging studies provide high-dimensional imaging phenotypes for understanding brain-related diseases and their causal relations with biological risk factors. While instrumental variable (IV) methods can address unmeasured confounding in such observational data, existing IV methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional imaging data, particularly in handling large-scale data and leveraging the intrinsic spatial structure of images. To address these challenges, we propose High-dimensional Functional-imaging Instrumental Variable Estimation (Hi-FIVE), a novel framework for estimating spatially varying causal effects when a majority of the candidate instruments may be locally invalid. We first establish identifiability conditions under which the spatial continuity of the causal effect surface propagates identification from regions where valid instruments form a plurality into regions where they do not, provided that invalid-IV effects switch on non-smoothly. Motivated by this result, Hi-FIVE combines penalized multivariate splines over triangulations for the causal surface and region-wise penalties for spatially localized invalid-IV effects, under an anchor constraint that keeps at least one relevant instrument valid on every simplex. A distributed algorithm parallelizes the computation over simplices for two- and three-dimensional images. We study the asymptotic properties of Hi-FIVE, establish consistency and pointwise asymptotic normality, and construct bootstrap-calibrated simultaneous confidence regions whose finite-sample coverage is evaluated through simulations. Hi-FIVE is illustrated with an analysis of the effect of phosphorylated tau on FDG-PET imaging in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, interpreted under the stated IV assumptions.

title: Economics of Selection in Ranking & Selection: Neither Fixed-Precision nor Fixed-Budget
summary: Ranking and selection (R&S) has evolved tremendously over the last several decades, with applications in agriculture, discrete optimization with computer simulation, clinical trial design, and other areas. We challenge a widely accepted classification of R&S procedures into two categories: fixed-precision and fixed-budget. We discuss a third class, economics-of-selection (EoS) procedures, which is conceptually distinct and is found in the extant literature on Bayesian hypothesis testing and simulation optimization. Procedures in this third class seek to optimally balance two quantities: the cost of learning about the performance of each alternative and the quality of the alternative ultimately selected on the basis of that learning. Fixed-precision and fixed-budget procedures tend to optimize one of these quantities while constraining the other. We clarify these differences and show why they matter. We then present new frequentist R&S procedures in this third category, including both two-stage procedures and a sequential heuristic, assuming Gaussian observations with either known or unknown variances. We find that EoS is not a question of Bayesian versus frequentist analysis, asymptotic versus finite-sample analysis, finite-stage versus fully sequential procedures, or comparing one mean with a standard versus comparing multiple alternatives. We identify opportunities for further R&S research.

title: Sufficient Dimension Reduction with Multimodal Predictor Objects
summary: We study the regression of a scalar response $Y$ on a Euclidean predictor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random predictor object $\mathcal{Z}$ in a general metric space under arbitrary structural dependence. We introduce a joint sufficient dimension reduction $(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathcal{G}_Z)$ constructed via a sequential conditional independence framework, which differs fundamentally from the ordinary central subspace of $Y \mid \mathbf{X}$. Methodologically, $\mathcal{Z}$ is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and a regularized kernel-response envelope model extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map. Partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction conditional on the first-stage coordinates. We establish root-$n$ consistency rates for the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer, alongside large-sample consistency for the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator. Simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the utility and flexibility of the proposed method.

title: Fractional-Order Hybrid SIR Forecasting of COVID-19 in Bangladesh and the United States: Memory Effects and Out-of-Sample Evaluation
comments: 23 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24057230
summary: Fractional-order epidemic models are often justified by memory, yet whether memory improves forecasts is rarely tested out of sample. We extend a hybrid SIR framework, in which a daily transmission rate is reconstructed from reported cases and then forecast, to Caputo fractional order $α\in(0,1]$. We prove well-posedness, conservation, positivity and a linearized threshold at disease-free states, and derive a Grünwald-Letnikov reconstruction that reduces exactly to the integer-order one at $α=1$. Our main theoretical result shows that for $α<1$ the influence of the unknown initial infectious count vanishes, but no faster than $t^{-α}$; after 332 daily steps it is about $4.4\times10^{8}$ times larger at $α=0.9$ than at $α=1$. In out-of-sample forecasting over 27 weekly origins, the effect of memory depends on the setting. In Bangladesh the integer order gives the lowest error for linear and constant-rate forecasts in 47 of 48 settings. In the United States, where reported cases reached about 18% of the population, a fractional order lowers the linear forecaster's error in all 12 comparisons in 2021 but raises the constant-rate forecaster's, with no difference significant after Holm adjustment. Against standard baselines, the SIR-based linear forecaster was more accurate than the classical SIR model and a neural network without SIR structure, and competitive with ARIMA: in the United States the fractional linear forecaster had the lowest error of all methods (seven-day MAPE 7.54% against 9.14% for ARIMA), whereas in Bangladesh ARIMA had the lowest MAPE, with no significant difference from ARIMA in either country. The choice of a fractional order should rest on out-of-sample evidence rather than in-sample fit.
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24057230

title: Testing isotropy of random fields with values in abstract spaces
summary: We study the problem of testing isotropy, i.e., distributional invariance under orthogonal transformations, for random fields taking values in abstract spaces. We propose a novel approach based on computing local directional characteristics, which are uniformly distributed under the assumption of isotropy. Our work is motivated by an application in material science, where we are testing the isotropy of function-valued porosity profiles of paper sheets, whose morphology is resolved by $μ$-CT imaging. While considerably more general, the presented methodology is competitive with existing isotropy tests for real-valued random fields.

title: A Bayesian approach for checking and estimating block designs in agricultural experiments
summary: Spatial blocking is a common technique used in designed agricultural experiments. Spatial blocking, however, requires important assumptions about the spatial dependence patterns in the field. Statistical models of blocked agricultural experiments often show spatial structure in the residuals, suggesting that the original model may benefit from additional assumptions regarding the spatial dependence patterns present in the field. We propose a Bayesian model for checking block membership and estimating spatial patterns missing in the original block design. Our model is particularly motivated by cases with mis-specified blocks. To accomplish this, we embed a regression tree within a Bayesian statistical model to estimate spatial effects with a block-like spatial structure. We illustrate the benefits of our model using simulated data mimicking four typical scenarios we have encountered in our applied experience in agricultural research and using two datasets generated from designed agricultural experiments. We found that our model may serve two purposes: validating the originally designed block layout, or mis-specified block-like spatial structures. Thus, our model provides researchers with a novel tool for analyzing data from designed agricultural experiments.

title: Cotangent-lift inference of stochastic microbial dynamics
summary: We study the parameter estimation for the stochastic logistic and Lotka--Volterra diffusions from discrete, irregularly spaced observations corrupted by measurement noise, a setting typical of microbiome time series. For the logistic equation, the growth rate acts as a time change and does not enter the stationary law, so it can be identified only from the temporal structure of the data. We prove that the maximum-likelihood estimator of the Euler scheme, with the observations taken as the states, coincides with the regression of log-increments on abundances used in the literature, and we characterise what this estimator cannot see under measurement noise: for the linearised dynamics, the law of consecutive pairs of observations is invariant along an explicit one-parameter family of relaxation rates and noise levels, and the regression converges to a limit set by the noise. Treating the true abundances as latent, we compute the likelihood with a Gaussian moment filter and show that measurement noise is precisely what couples the filter states across samples. The exact gradient is then the backward recursion of the discrete cotangent lift, whose cost, two to three likelihood evaluations, does not depend on the number of parameters, and we give the covector map of each filter step in closed form. In simulations, the latent estimator recovers the relaxation times, noise levels and interaction strengths that the regression biases, while larger communities require prior information on the interactions. In gut microbiome time series it attributes most of the variability of a dominant genus to measurement noise and estimates its relaxation time at about $64$ hours, with a large standard error.

title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
summary:
Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised.
  We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation.
  Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks.
  The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

title: Bayesian Multinomial Logistic Normal Additive Regression for Microbiome Data Analysis
summary:
Longitudinal microbiome studies often seek to separate background temporal variation from nonlinear perturbation-associated dynamics while accounting for the count-compositional nature of sequencing data. We introduce \textit{MultiAddGPs}, a semi-parametric Bayesian multinomial logistic-normal framework that combines linear effects with additive Gaussian process components. We first prove that MultiAddGPs remain within the Marginally Latent Matrix-T Process class (MLTP) and derive the collapsed and uncollapsed representations needed for scalable inference with the Collapse--Uncollapse (CU) sampler. We then develop a back-sampling procedure for efficient posterior inference on the individual additive components. We further develop approximate maximum marginal likelihood and penalized maximum marginal likelihood procedures for hyperparameter estimation in this broader class of models. In simulations, MultiAddGPs provides accurate posterior inference and calibrated uncertainty while scaling more effectively than existing GP-based additive alternatives. Applications to two longitudinal microbiome studies demonstrate how the model separates background temporal variation from intervention-associated dynamics, including travel-associated perturbations in a human gut time series and starvation effects
  in an artificial gut system. Our methods are implemented in the \textit{fido} package on CRAN.

title: Nonzero-Sum Stochastic Exit Games with Singular Belief Dynamics
summary: We study a two-player nonzero-sum stochastic exit game with asymmetric information. Each firm chooses the time to exit a duopoly and, conditional on remaining active, when to exit a monopoly. The asymmetry stems from privately observed exit values, while profit flows are driven by a general one-dimensional diffusion. Allowing for exit from monopoly induces singular dynamics of the associated belief process, so we construct it as a limit of regular approximations. The underlying dynamics are not described by a system of SDEs, which requires a new mathematical approach. We construct a symmetric Nash equilibrium in which the duopoly exit is a hitting time of the belief process while the monopoly exit is described through the underlying diffusion. Our equilibrium exhibits novel phenomena: the market may be abandoned by both firms in finite time (market collapse), and firms with heterogeneous exit values may optimally exit simultaneously (clustering). These features are absent when monopoly is always preferred to exit.

title: Asian option valuation under price impact
summary: We develop a model for arithmetic and geometric Asian option valuation with external order flow and dealer execution costs. We first formulate it as a discrete model and then obtain its continuous time scaling limit. We derive an explicit geometric Asian option formula under a consistent price system and formulate the dealer's bid and ask through utility indifference with constrained stock trading. We identify sufficient conditions for finite reservation prices and prove absence of arbitrage under the dealer's stock trading rules. Increasing initial inventory lowers both the reservation bid and the ask in the cases studied. In the finite-step calculations, higher temporary costs and greater risk aversion widen the spread for both payoffs, with a smaller change in the midpoint of the quotes.

AI.title_translation: 考虑价格影响下的亚洲期权定价
AI.tldr: 本文提出了一种考虑价格影响和交易商执行成本的亚洲期权定价与报价模型，分析了库存、成本及风险厌恶对价差的影响。
AI.motivation: 传统的期权定价模型往往忽略了市场价格影响（price impact）和交易商的执行成本，无法真实反映大额订单或流动性受限市场中的期权定价与做市商报价机制。
AI.method: 首先建立离散模型，随后推导其连续时间尺度极限；在自洽价格系统下推导显式几何亚洲期权公式；利用具有约束股票交易的效用无差异方法构建交易商的买卖报价。
AI.result: 识别出了存在有限保留价格的充分条件，证明了在交易商股票交易规则下的无套利性；发现增加初始库存会降低保留买价和卖价；更高的临时成本和更大的风险 aversion 会扩大买卖价差，而报价中点变化较小。
AI.conclusion: 研究成功建立了一个考虑价格影响和交易商成本的亚洲期权定价与报价框架，证明了无套利性质，并揭示了初始库存、交易成本和风险厌恶程度对买卖价差及保留价格的具体影响。
AI.translation: 我们开发了一个用于算术和几何亚洲期权估值的模型，该模型考虑了外部订单流和做市商的执行成本。我们首先将其建模为一个离散模型，然后获取其连续时间尺度极限。我们在自洽的价格系统下推导出了一个显式的几何亚洲期权公式，并通过具有受限股票交易的效用无差异性来制定做市商的买入价和卖出价。我们确定了存在有限保留价格的充分条件，并证明了在做市商股票交易规则下不存在套利。在所研究的案例中，增加初始库存会降低保留买价和卖价。在有限步计算中，更高的临时成本和更大的风险厌恶程度会扩大这两种收益的价差，而报价中点的变化较小。
AI.summary: 该论文开发了一个针对算术和几何亚洲期权的估值模型，考虑了外部订单流和交易商执行成本。通过离散建模及其连续极限，推导了几何亚洲期权的显式公式，并基于约束股票交易的效用无差异原理确定了买卖报价，同时分析了初始库存、交易成本和风险厌恶对报价的影响。
AI.keywords: 亚洲期权, 价格影响, 效用无差异, 无套利, 做市商报价
AI.comments: 该论文将市场微观结构中的价格影响（price impact）与传统亚洲期权定价相结合，通过引入外部订单流和交易商执行成本，提供了一个更为现实的期权定价与做市商报价模型，对于理解流动性及交易摩擦对期权价值的影响具有重要理论价值。
